comments.body:
## Weekly Sync 10/19 - 10/23 **Agenda:** - Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data - Deduplication details - Decontamination plan - Release Plan ---
Investigation of how RoPE impacted the LLM Data Last week's worry: the last ~3k WARCs of the lpv11 10k extraction might have run with the vllm-tpu RoPE bug. **They did not. No LLM data we use was affected.** **Why:** the bug lives in tpu-inference's JAX re-implementation of Qwen3. Our Qwen3-8B extractor loads from a `gs://` checkpoint through the runai streamer, and the JAX Qwen3 port has no streaming weight loader, so vLLM's `auto` setting resolves to the PyTorch-via-torchax path, which is correct. **Only models loaded from the HF cache or local disk took the JAX path. In our work that was only ReScraper.** **Verified three ways:** - Code path and old job logs: every Qwen3-8B run used the torchax path (lpv11 10k extraction, gap-fill, WebMainBench 7,809, devset, classifier scoring). - Reruns with the implementation pinned to torchax: devset 99.8% decision agreement; WebMainBench shard 00 F1 .6400 vs .6422; 1k lpv11 pages 626/975 byte-identical, median similarity 0.994 on the rest. - Quality unchanged on the 1k rerun: major hallucinations 1.1% vs 1.6%, within judge noise (51 vs 52 flagged on identical pages); SRS 2.64 vs 2.66. **The 8M hero data runs no LLM at inference time:** it is resiliparse-rs extraction, then a fastText gate, then a ModernBERT classifier. The LLM only produced the distillation labels, and those came from the correct path.
> [!TIP] > False alarm for our data: only ReScraper (loaded from local disk) hit the bug. Every Qwen3-8B extraction ran on the correct path, which logs and reruns confirm. ---
Deduplication details | Stage | Docs | Characters | Tokens (llama3) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Extracted (8,582,115 WARCs) | 61.21B | 341.8T | ≈80.6T | | After exact dedup | 21.84B | 133.9T | ≈31.6T | | After fuzzy dedup (hero cluster method, c075) | **9.95B** | **72.7T** | **17.15T** | Characters are exact at every stage. The final token count is measured; the first two use the final corpus's 4.239 chars/token. - **17.15T llama3 tokens** (72.7T chars, 26.5 TB). The refit after the 2M run projected 16.9T (15.7–18.9T); the projections made at 500k (21.8–25.0T) were too high. - 64% of extracted records were exact duplicates, confirmed to be the same pages recrawled across crawls. - By source: **CC-MAIN 16.68T**, **CC-NEWS 0.21T** (tagged `CC-NEWS-YYYY-MM`, so it can be mixed separately), **CC-SUPPLEMENTAL 7.8B**. - Random-sample viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/9Wp8sdhFwC7xmRqz74ddpx
> [!TIP] > Dedup is done: **17.15T tokens** from 8.58M WARCs, in line with the post-2M projection. The hero run used ~25T. ---
Decontamination plan Full walkthrough with examples: https://claude.ai/artifact/FPrunN93nfrApC6j4hcgSN **How Marin's decon works.** Take the test questions and answers from every benchmark we report (the 9 Artificial Analysis benchmarks plus the lm-eval tasks in Marin's eval suite). Split each training doc into paragraphs. If at least half of a paragraph's 13-word runs also appear in the eval text, the doc is removed. Phrases that are common all over the web are ignored, so boilerplate can't trigger a removal. The version the hero run used (v3) adds one more check for short paragraphs (3–12 words), which are too short to contain a 13-word run: a short paragraph that exactly matches a short line from the evals also removes the doc. That check is meant to catch short eval answers, but it also matches ordinary lines like "2 years ago" or "Lana Del Rey". Marin changed this after the hero run (v4, PR #8327, Sept 24): a paragraph now needs at least two different eval phrases in it to count, so a single short line can't remove a doc by itself. **Where we are.** Every doc in the pool has been checked. Picking a rule now just means one ~3 h filter run, then an ~18 h re-tokenize. **Tokens each rule would remove** (estimated from a 24k-doc audit sample): | Rule | Eval set | Docs removed | Tokens removed | |---|---|---:|---:| | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's + 118 tasks the hero failed to load | ~11M | ~87B (0.5%) | | v3 (hero run's rule) | hero's | ~5M | ~40B (0.23%) | | v4 (Marin `main` today) | hero's + 118 tasks | ~0.46M | ~8B (0.05%) | The two v3 numbers will drop somewhat: I'm re-running the boilerplate count with the hero's sample size (1M docs per crawl; my first pass used ~80k). **Problems with the hero run's decon:** 1. **gsm8k was probably never checked.** 118 of the lm-eval tasks, including gsm8k, truthfulqa, winogrande, boolq and triviaqa, failed to load in the hero's eval set because their old dataset names break with the `datasets` version the hero branch uses. The pipeline skips tasks that fail to load instead of stopping. This is based on the eval set's manifest in us-central2. **Not yet checked against the CoreWeave copy that production actually used.** 2. **The short-line check mostly removes harmless pages.** On our data, ~95% of v3 removals come from a single short line like "2 years ago" or "Mechanism of Action", and none of the 40 I read by hand were contamination. Our extracted text has lots of standalone short lines (96% of docs have one, against 25–77% in Nemotron-CC), so this hits us harder than it hit the hero data. v4 fixes the second problem. On the audit sample it still caught every real overlap we found (SQuAD passages, wikiHow/HellaSwag, MATH problems, paper abstracts) and only let through stray short phrases and two generic LSAT question stems. **Decisions:** 1. **Eval set:** add the 118 tasks the hero missed? 2. **Rule:** v3 (~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages) or v4 (~8B tokens, same real catches)? 3. **ACTION ITEM:** Check with Will about the potential GSM8K gap in decontamination
> [!TIP] > Every doc has been checked against the evals. The hero run's rule (v3) would remove ~87B tokens, mostly harmless pages; Marin's current rule (v4) removes ~8B with the same real catches. The hero run also perhaps checked 117 fewer tasks. ---
Release Plan **Need to run the embedding and scaling ladder**: Reached out to Will to discuss this. I have all my data in `us-central2` ready to run a scaling ladder! Just want to figure out pointers on what to run and if I need to do control against Nemotron or if that has already been run somewhere. **Otherwise after decontamination the data is ready to go!**
> [!TIP] > After decontamination we are ready to release! ---

comments.body:
## Weekly Sync 10/26 - 10/30 **Agenda:** - Decontamination Conclusion - Discussions with CCF - Release Timeline ---
Decontamination Conclusion Artifact Viewer: https://claude.ai/artifact/35vPM8xar7mPgConPqKtkY Our investigation turned up that it seems several datasets were not fully decontaminated in the marin data. In our direct message discussions we determined that we should decontaminate against: **lm_eval, AAII, Paloma, Uncheatable Eval, and LIMA**. Last week I reported that decontamination with Marin's Rules would remove 8B tokens. Actually running it for benchmarks only removed 3B tokens. Adding in Paloma, Uncheatable and LIMA originally brought this up to 20B tokens. (Note these datasets are just 66M tokens - mostly Paloma). **REMINDER:** The Marin Decontamination rule put simply - **A document is removed when any blank-line-separated paragraph has at least half of its 13-gram phrases** (every overlapping 13-gram window, excluding common _**boilerplate phrases**_ and phrases with no letters) **found in an eval set, with at least two different phrases matching**, or when the whole document is a single matching 3–12-word line, or has only one usable phrase and it matches. **What counts as boilerplate?** a phrase counted as boilerplate (and was ignored in matching) if it appeared in at least 0.5% of the first 5,000 docs of any single crawl, or in at least 50 docs across at least 3 crawls within a sample of the first 1M docs per crawl. I noticed some problems with decontaminating against document-level based evals which we weren't seeing from the benchmark evals: Code is really impacted by this!! TWO REASONS: - Comments - Imports Comments vary from language to language. People paste license text into files, but the comment style matches the language that they are writing the code in. So sometimes this license text is not marked as boilerplate simply because of a few comment characters that break the count. Imports are fairly ubiquitous in a given language HOWEVER, the order of imports is not something consistent. Since there is exponentially many orderings to reasonably import your files certain import orders are never marked as boilerplate. **We were discarding a lot of useful code data!** To fix this I did something simple. I am not super satisfied with this but feels like this is a reasonable action given we don't want to launch a whole new project on just fixing decontamination right now. **New rule for boilerplate:** A phrase counts as boilerplate (and is ignored in matching) if it appears in at least 0.5% of the first 5,000 docs of any single crawl, in at least 50 docs across at least 3 crawls within a sample of the first 1M docs per crawl, in at least 1,000 docs across at least 3 crawls in the full pool, **or in at least 100 files of StarCoderData.** Starcoder data is just programming data in 86 languages. My hope was that this would at least cover more of the license files and import orders even if this isn't a _complete_ solution. Ultimately with these rules we ended up removing 12B tokens. Note still most of this comes from the validation datasets (since the benchmarks removed 3B tokens) **I ran this updated version and have the data ready for upload to the Common Crawl Foundation.**
---
Discussions with Common Crawl Foundation The CCF gave me a small bucket to test sharing the data with them, and all seems to work, so just waiting to hear back from them about a larger bucket and if the file format is good. ``` Atlantic CC release format (as agreed with CCF; part/row-group sizes pending their final OK) Location: s3://commoncrawl/projects//v1.0/parquet/crawl=/part-NNNNN-of-MMMMM.parquet plus v1.0/_manifest.json (record and part counts per crawl) Versioning: v1.0 = this release; appending new crawls = v1.1; changing the pipeline/algorithm = v2.0 Crawls: one prefix per crawl (249: CC-MAIN-YYYY-WW, CC-NEWS-YYYY-MM, CC-SUPPLEMENTAL). Dedup is global, so each doc appears once, under the crawl its kept copy came from. Format: Parquet, zstd level 9, ~300 MB parts, 10k-row row groups. No JSONL. Size: 9,950,417,677 records, 87,203 parts, 22.75 TB Fields: record_id string WARC-Record-ID (UUID) of the source record url string source page URL crawl string crawl the WARC belongs to (e.g. CC-MAIN-2025-08, CC-NEWS-2016-08) warc_hash string first 12 hex chars of sha256(WARC file path) text string extracted main text (resiliparse-rs, light markdown) fasttext_score float quality stage 1 (fastText imitating the LLM filter's keep/drop decision) pooled_prob float quality stage 2 (90M pooled-transformer classifier) modernbert_prob float? quality stage 3 (Ettin-68M classifier); null if stage 2 kept the doc outright exact_copies int docs in the pre-dedup pool with identical text (1 = unique) fuzzy_cluster_size int size of the doc's near-duplicate component (~4.56B = the one giant chained component) Processing: extraction -> 3-stage quality cascade -> exact + fuzzy dedup (c075) -> decontamination (Marin v4 rule, eval set = benchmarks + Paloma + Uncheatable + LIMA; 1.35M docs / ~12B tokens removed) ```
---
Release Timeline/Ideas If I hear back from CCF folks soon I think we should **release next Monday**! I have some ideas for the release: - Twitter Thread - Website (http://atlantic-cc.org/) - Arxiv (Add ReScraper results and update Figure 2 - some spacing improvements) - Marin Blog? What would need to be done for that to be possible? Should I just do my own blog? (Perhaps this can be done in a week or two when we have the scaling ladder, this would be more Marin-specific) The blog would be more about showing data samples and intuitively explaining the data. Other interesting ideas: - Maybe we should release subsets (DCLM-400M-1x, DCLM-1B-1x, etc.) for all the people who may want to compare against our data on academic compute scales. - Release a small sample viewer anyone can view like 100 docs (maybe extra data check for legal)
---

## Weekly Sync 11/2-11/6 **Agenda:** - Baseline Fairness Check - Scaling experiment updates - Release updates ---
Baseline Fairness Check This weekend while processing some stuff for Atlantic-CC I had a realization about how we ran our baselines. I think this is okay, but wanted to run it by you all in case you can think of a more reasonable way to do this. **For every other release:** We take the fully released version and filter down to just what they got from the ~10k WARC files. **For GC-Cascade/GC-LLM:** We run it just on those 10k WARC files. The problem is that we are essentially working with globally deduplicated baselines, but "locally" deduplicated for our method. **How significant of a concern is this?** I'm not certain... now I can actually do this for Atlantic-CC and the effect seems pretty dramatic. **91.65B tokens -> 23.48B tokens**. YIKES! However there is reason to believe we aren't this unfair against the baselines actually. I set off reproducing DCLM from their code instead of our "backwards filtering" way and this was the result: **7.33B tokens -> 9.47B tokens**. Not _as_ bad. Also there is reason to believe we aren't that harsh against Fineweb. Fineweb did local-deduplication instead of global deduplication: Ultimately I still wanted to run an experiment to get to the bottom of if we are being unfair to our baselines. And even still I am not sure so this is why I want to open this up to a discussion. Two important caveats: **these are unmixed**, and **this heavily punishes atlantic-cc**. We are super aggressive with dedup in a way that almost no other dataset release is. The marin global dedup is extremely punishing. Look at DCLM numbers for comparison: In our case deduplication took us from 80.6T tokens to 17.1T tokens! But still this isn't a great look to have our baselines be treated differently and when we apply it on our data it flips some of the results.... Any thoughts about how we should proceed with this?
> [!TIP] > I wanted to make sure we are reporting baselines fairly. I think with all of this there are some tradeoffs that need to be made, and I just want to make sure we are making the most fair decisions we can given the circumstances. ---
Scaling experiment updates We finished embedding the full deduplicated, decontaminated 8M-WARC pool (9.95B documents) with Harrier and labeled every document with the hero run's models: 5,000 fine and 40 coarse domain clusters, content type, and the calibrated quality score with its 5 buckets. All 9,950,417,677 label rows line up with the embeddings, and all 200 domain × quality cells used by the hero mixture have documents. We are now splitting the pool's existing 17.1T-token tokenization into those 200 cells (a pilot on 13M documents checked out), which should finish within a couple of hours, after which we choose mixture weights over the cells (reuse the hero's or retune).
> [!TIP] > Embedding is done, I want to discuss next steps with Will and understand if I need to run anything with respect to Nemotron comparisons/data mixing etc. ---
Release updates **Code** - Atlantic-CC: https://github.com/marin-community/atlantic-cc/tree/main - Generative Curation (Paper Reproduction): https://github.com/marin-community/generative-curation **Models/Extractors** - Custom Resiliparse: https://github.com/marin-community/atlantic-cc-resiliparse - FastText: https://huggingface.co/marin-community/atlantic-cc-fasttext - Pooled Transformer: https://huggingface.co/marin-community/atlantic-cc-pooled-transformer - ModernBERT: https://huggingface.co/marin-community/atlantic-cc-modernbert **Data** - Atlantic-CC Sample (all EXTREMELY permissively licensed): https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/Atlantic-CC-Sample - The rest will go to Common Crawl's huggingface. They already have all the data, but just working with Malte to get it up on huggingface. Will eventually look something like this: https://huggingface.co/buckets/commoncrawl/commoncrawl - I have produced the academic subsets: This is all ready for hosting! I just need to finish working with the Common Crawl team on this. _The bucket (s3://commoncrawl/projects/atlantic-cc/v1.0/) already has all 17.1T tokens!_ **Paper** https://www.overleaf.com/read/tzzfngmmyqsp#daf616 Changelog: - [ ] Added links to huggingface/github to header of document - [x] Figure1: Updated Real and Projected Token Counts after Atlantic-CC Run - [ ] Revised introduction to be more interesting - [x] Relaxed figure spacing throughout - [x] Added Rescraper to Related Works section - [ ] Figure 2 updated with example of extraction failure and example of filtering failure (separate) - [x] Figure 4 updated with latest runs (a few models were still training at the time of submission, no findings changed) - [x] Figure 5 updated with latest runs (a few models were still training at the time of submission, no findings changed) - [ ] Table 3 updated with Rescraper results - [ ] Table 4 updated with Rescraper results - [ ] Ablations for contribution of extraction vs filtering added to Appendix - [ ] Acknowledgements **Twitter** - https://docs.google.com/document/d/1L6xGPGXnSq6m4TLGBrw7C7zwMvqKWcAKEi96c2kpGMk/edit?usp=sharing **Website**: http://atlantic-cc.org/ Still need to update the site, but would be great if it could organize all of these links since there are so many for this project. **Random TODOs**: - [ ] Don't forget to update the start of this GitHub issue with the latest definition of done Anything else you can think of and any way that we can make this all clear to people (I don't want to dump everything and people are completely lost where to look).
> [!TIP] > We are almost ready for release! ---

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
Add three selected public text-only subsets of [LAB-Bench v1](https://openathena.ai/bio-evals/benchmarks/lab-bench) to Marin's vendored Evalchemy and expose each component separately in EvalDash. This prepares LAB-Bench for a proposed in-distribution (ID) development evaluation under the [Marin evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Canonical policy adoption remains a separate decision after validation.

Scope:

| Component | Public questions | Evaluation key |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| ProtocolQA | 108 | `lab-bench-protocolqa` |
| SeqQA | 600 | `lab-bench-seqqa` |
| CloningScenarios | 33 | `lab-bench-cloning` |

Support all 741 public questions from the pinned [dataset revision](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench/tree/5c77cec648430f30611808808861eb86f81d5eaa); routine policy selection remains open. The model receives text and generates a multiple-choice answer without browsing, code execution, or other external tools. SeqQA therefore measures unaided sequence reasoning.

Implementation decisions and alternatives considered (2026-10-26):

These choices define the current draft implementation; they do not constitute team approval for canonical evaluation-policy adoption.

| Decision | Alternative considered | Reason for the current choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start with the three public text-only components, without tools. | Add retrieval, vision, or tool-enabled tasks in the same integration. | Establish a bounded no-tools baseline. The omitted components and requirements for revisiting them are listed below. |
| Preserve separate ProtocolQA, SeqQA and CloningScenarios scores, with SeqQA subtask diagnostics. | Publish only one aggregate LAB-Bench score, or hide component scores inside one evaluation record. | Components measure different capabilities and need separately comparable histories. No canonical aggregate or ranking weight has been agreed. |
| Use generated answers with reasoning allowed. | Score answer-letter log probabilities without generation. | Evaluate reasoning followed by an answer, using the existing generation path. Log-probability scoring would define a different protocol. |
| Remove the author harness's added abstention choice; report accuracy, standard error and sample counts. | Retain abstention-aware precision and attempted-answer coverage. | The current goal is forced-choice capability measurement. This deliberately gives up reproduction of the original uncertainty-calibration protocol. |
| Request a final `Answer: X` and reuse the shared MCQ extractor. | Require the original answer tags and maintain a LAB-Bench-specific grader and reducer. | Follow existing Evalchemy conventions and avoid benchmark-specific formatting machinery. Answers the shared grader cannot extract count as incorrect; deviations from the requested format may still be recoverable. API delivery failures remain ungraded. |
| Use deterministic per-item choice shuffling and pin the dataset and scorer. | Reproduce the author harness's exact permutations. | Preserve reproducible Marin runs without claiming exact historical score comparability. |
| Add the benchmark within vendored Evalchemy, with minimal Marin registration. | Add a Harbor adaptation, dedicated launcher suite, dashboard group, and general tutorial changes. | These direct no-tools questions fit Evalchemy. Existing registration and dashboard behavior provide the three component entries. Keep benchmark-specific protocol documentation close to the adapter. |
| Use shared output-budget resolution, allowing explicit run/model overrides. | Hard-code an 8192-token LAB-Bench output cap. | Avoid a benchmark-specific budget constant. The eventual policy budget is still open; the 32768-token GLM diagnostic cap is not a policy default. |
| Keep native thinking-token control as a candidate run setting; defer explicit continuation machinery. | Add a second model request or a forced final-answer instruction to rescue remaining truncations. | The same-question GLM diagnostic improved from 6/21 to 15/21 with a native cap. Two remaining failures repeated reasoning in the answer channel. Further continuation complexity has uncertain benefit; no LAB-Bench-specific workaround or policy default is adopted. |
| Retain the dataset's answers and scientific conventions. | Adjudicate or repair possible scientific ambiguities, including ORF conventions. | Scientific benchmark repair is outside the current integration scope. No answer-key changes or scientific exclusions have been made. |
| Reuse shared runtime/grader tests, with focused coverage only where behavior changes. | Add a separate extensive test suite for every benchmark registration. | Test adaptation and shared behavior that can fail without duplicating implementation details or creating a mandatory per-benchmark suite. |

Open decisions for the team before policy adoption:

- **Suitability and protocol:** Are these three components appropriate ID development evaluations, and are the forced-choice and formatting departures acceptable? Implementation choices above remain subject to this policy decision.
- **SeqQA subset size:** Use 75 or 150 questions (5 or 10 from each of the 15 subtasks) for routine evaluation? The integration continues to support the full public dataset; the subset size remains open.
- **Reasoning and output limits:** Adopt an 8192-token thinking cap and 16384-token total output cap for GLM evaluations? This native-budget candidate improved the same 21-question diagnostic from 6/21 to 15/21 and reduced truncations from 14 to 2; detailed results and limitations are below. It is not yet an agreed policy default or a validated cross-model setting. Explicit continuation machinery remains deferred.
- **Runtime and cost:** Measure evaluator wall-clock time per component, excluding scheduler wait and model-server startup; retain model, reasoning/output limits, concurrency and timeout settings. Report mean and sample standard deviation across the evaluated cohort following the [evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Separate per-request/trial limits from overall job limits and small-smoke timings from full-panel measurements. Decide whether the measured runtime warrants subsetting or tighter generation budgets.
- **Aggregation and ranking weight:** Decide between keeping only component-level reporting and defining an explicit aggregate. Pooling all questions heavily weights SeqQA; including all three dashboard columns also gives the benchmark three ranking entries. No canonical weighting is chosen.
- **Failures and retries:** Answers the shared grader cannot extract and reasoning-only output-budget exhaustion score incorrect under the current grader. API/transport failures remain ungraded. Agree on bounded infrastructure retries, completion requirements, and how retry provenance is reported; do not silently retry wrong or truncated answers. Luna's combined result explicitly identifies two separately generated diagnostic retries.
- **Validation required for adoption:** Direct endpoint runs establish prompt/grader results but do not establish the full native Marin → Evalchemy → EvalDash path. Complete that integration validation before claiming readiness for canonical panels.

Detailed results, the collapsed SeqQA subtask table, and archived launcher code are in the [Luna results record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10575#issuecomment-6423403346).

Deferred scope and rationale:

| Item | Why deferred | Requirements for a follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool-enabled versions of the selected subsets, especially SeqQA | Tools change the measured capability from unaided reasoning to performance with an agent and its tools. Establish the no-tools baseline first. | Define a separately named protocol with fixed tools, agent, network access and execution budgets; validate a Harbor task adaptation and retain tool traces. |
| LitQA2 (199), SuppQA (82), DbQA (520) | These target literature, supplementary-material and database retrieval. A no-tools score is possible, but would not establish retrieval capability. | Specify literature/corpus access, supplement handling and database versions or snapshots, plus tool and network policy. Validate source availability and scoring under that protocol. |
| FigQA (181), TableQA (244) | Both supply images, including TableQA's tables. They require a vision-capable evaluation path and model cohort. | Preserve image inputs and validate the multimodal route. Treat the existing Harbor FigQA agent protocol separately from direct tool-free image answering; it does not cover TableQA. |
| LABBench2 | It is a distinct benchmark with different tasks and grading, requiring its own scope and integration assessment. | Review dataset access, subset selection and native evaluators before proposing a separate addition. |
| Authors' private holdout | It is not part of the public release available for this implementation. | Obtain author-approved access and evaluation terms before considering its use. |

Counts refer to the public [LAB-Bench dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench). These deferrals do not assign the omitted subsets an ID or OOD designation.

Implementation and protocol details:

[Draft PR #10582](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10582) implements `marin-labbench-no-tools-v3` with one shared loader/prompt builder, three Evalchemy registrations and three Marin evaluation configurations. Evalchemy's sources are part of the vendored runtime; Harbor's adapter generators are maintained separately, and its existing LAB-Bench adapter covers FigQA only. EvalDash's [measurement layer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/86fc7b67c9/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/eval_measurements.py#L254) uses one headline measurement per registered evaluation name, motivating the three entries.

The shared `letter_choice` grader uses HLE's deterministic extractor, without an LLM fallback. It prefers provider final-answer content and strips explicit thinking blocks. Normally completed reasoning-only responses remain eligible for extraction; reasoning-only truncations score zero. Within the selected text, it uses the first answer-prefixed letter, then the last isolated letter as a fallback. The final-content correction also affects HLE and GPQA Diamond. Earlier v2 results and separately labeled v3 rescoring are preserved.

Choice shuffling uses the seed, subset and item ID. Shared output-budget resolution honors explicit run/model limits; otherwise it uses remaining context after prompt reserve and margins. The checked-in configuration requests one response per item, temperature 0, seed 42 and thinking enabled. Effective run overrides must be recorded. Earlier tagged-answer/abstention runs are not comparable to this variant.

GLM native-thinking-cap diagnostic (2026-10-30):

Repeated the identical 21 questions from the [32k-total diagnostic](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10575#issuecomment-6528781433): one per SeqQA subtask and three each from ProtocolQA and CloningScenarios. The launcher checked that question IDs, messages and targets matched before generation. Medium reasoning, temperature 0, top_p 1, seed 42, concurrency 1 and no automatic retries were retained. The new request sets `thinking_token_budget=8192` and `max_tokens=16384`; the earlier run had only a 32768-token total cap.

| Component / measurement | 32k total, no explicit thinking cap | 8k thinking / 16k total |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| ProtocolQA | 2/3 | 3/3 |
| SeqQA | 4/15 | 11/15 |
| CloningScenarios | 0/3 | 1/3 |
| Total correct | 6/21 | 15/21 |
| Output-limit truncations | 14/21 | 2/21 |
| Request failures | 0 | 0 |
| Iris task runtime including setup | 27m11s | 10m57s |

All 21 new responses were saved and graded. This is a small diagnostic comparison across separate runs, not a full GLM baseline or a controlled isolation of the thinking-cap effect: both reasoning and total limits changed, and the endpoint deployment was not pinned across dates. Execution again used direct service requests with Evalchemy prompts and the shared v3 grader, not native Marin → EvalDash validation.

The two remaining truncations were CloningScenarios items `8cd98408-8672-4330-911e-57bff9ec334a` (sequencing-primer selection) and `908754dd-ffea-48f6-a969-25e954bfe68f` (restriction-digest fragments). Each used exactly 8192 reported reasoning tokens and 16384 total output tokens. The answer channel continued the interrupted reasoning mid-sentence, including exact repeated passages of at least 5232 and 6119 characters respectively, without a final choice. The fallback extractor selected incidental invalid-option letters S and R; both scores remain zero. Native budget enforcement limits the reasoning channel but does not guarantee that answer text stops reasoning.

Decision: defer two-stage continuation and explicit conclusion-prompt machinery. Retain the native cap as a candidate evaluation setting pending team policy agreement; keep remaining failures incorrect and preserve earlier results. No model reruns were made for the trace audit. The [Ortet procedure](https://ortet.ai/blog/open-models-in-health/#evaluation-configurations) motivated the investigation, but its two-request fallback has not been implemented here.

[Saved results](s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/eval-validation/labbench-10575/glm-thinking8k-total16k-20261030/graded.json), [trace audit](s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/eval-validation/labbench-10575/glm-thinking8k-total16k-20261030/truncation-audit.json), and [launcher archive](s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/eval-validation/labbench-10575/glm-thinking8k-total16k-20261030/launcher.tar.gz) are retained separately; launcher MD5 is `243c22eae2912d2901c9de75f7456db9`. These links require Marin object-storage access. The preceding single-request capability probe independently reported exactly 64 reasoning tokens with a 64-token cap and returned a correct final answer.

Current full-panel evidence:

Full Luna high run and diagnostic retries (2026-10-26): all 741 requests were attempted with eight concurrent standard OpenRouter requests. The original run retained 739 graded responses: ProtocolQA 78/108, SeqQA 507/599, CloningScenarios 26/32. One SeqQA completion exhausted its output budget and scored zero. Two outer API responses failed JSON decoding, leaving those questions ungraded; the original run remains marked partial. Runtime was 1h13m50s including setup and reported model cost was $1.64005307, excluding any unreported charges for the failed responses.

The original diagnostic capture was insufficient: it decoded JSON before saving the HTTP body and did not retain headers or the decoder position. The exact cause of those two failures cannot be recovered. A separate diagnostic run repeated only indices 652 (SeqQA restriction-fragment lengths) and 723 (CloningScenarios), using unchanged request bodies at concurrency one, no automatic retries, and raw-body/status/header capture before parsing. Both returned HTTP 200, valid JSON and normal stops. SeqQA was correct; Cloning was incorrect. Diagnostic model cost was $0.004148025. This failed to reproduce the original problem and does not establish a provider or model root cause.

A separately labeled result combining 739 original responses with these two new attempts yields ProtocolQA 78/108 (72.2%), SeqQA 508/600 (84.7%), and CloningScenarios 26/33 (78.8%). Original failures and scores remain unchanged. The prompt messages, choices and targets match the GLM run. Done when:

- [ ] The pinned public dataset yields the expected component counts and stable item IDs. Correct-choice labels and grading metadata remain hidden; correct answer text appears as an unlabeled member of the shuffled choices.

Reuse shared grader/runtime tests and add only focused dataset-adaptation coverage; verify choice/target alignment and verify the corrected final-content extraction on saved responses before accepting baseline scores.

These are scores for the Marin forced-choice variant, not a reproduction of the authors' uncertainty-calibration protocol. Dataset answers and scientific conventions were left unchanged.

Execution used a private Iris launcher making direct OpenRouter requests with Evalchemy's prompt builder and grader. It does **not** establish native Marin launcher → EvalDash validation. PR #10582 remains draft.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 Compared **1,967 public LAB-Bench v1 rows with 1,912 LABBench2 rows**, including v2 sequence attachments and protocol PDFs, to assess overlap relevant to using v1 as ID and v2 as a held-out evaluation.

**The overlap varies by category.** LitQA contains confirmed reused questions. SeqQA and ProtocolQA retain substantial skill overlap, even when the inputs or answers change. CloningQA shifts toward complete protocol design. Shared papers or vector sequences alone do not establish duplicate questions.

The tables combine automated measurements with direct inspection of questions and reference answers. Short quotations come from the [LABBench2 paper, §2](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2); the semantic assessments are ours. Counts are identified overlaps, not exhaustive semantic-duplication rates.

| V1 → V2 category | Paper’s description | Measured overlap and semantic assessment |
|---|---|---|
| LitQA2 → **LitQA3** | “ported from LitQA2”: some adapted questions; most are new. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **≥43/168 (25.6%) confirmed carryovers:** 19 identical and 24 reworded questions. Other inspected questions seek new facts using the same literature-retrieval skills. |
| FigQA → **FigQA2** | “all new questions”, with image, PDF and retrieval variants. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **30/101 (29.7%)** retrieval rows share papers with v1. Inspected pairs generally ask for different measurements using familiar figure-reading skills. **One strong same-fact candidate**, pending image-context verification. |
| TableQA → **TableQA2** | New questions and the same three input variants described above. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **86/100 (86%)** retrieval rows share papers with v1. Strong continuity in table-reading skills, often with a different target cell or comparison. **One strong same-fact candidate**, pending image-context verification. |
| SuppQA → **SuppQA2** | “carried forward”: supplementary-material retrieval in open-response form. [§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1) | **1/125** shares a source and ID but asks a different question. Same skill—retrieving primers, parameters and other experimental details—with generally different targets in the inspected sample. |
| DbQA → **DbQA2** | Broader and more specific database coverage (paraphrased). [§2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS2) | No exact-question, ID or source-identifier matches across **86 rows**. Broader tasks across **43 named sources**, but continuing database skills; ClinVar and Ensembl appear in both. No obvious same-fact reuse in the inspected comparisons. |
| SeqQA → **SeqQA2** | “a similar approach”: 20 templates × 20 instances, including new subcategories and file/retrieval inputs. [§2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS3) | **40/400 (10%)** share DNA segments ≥100 bases with v1: all Gibson-primer and restriction-cloning primer-design rows. **Substantial skill overlap** in GC content, restriction analysis, ORFs and primers, alongside new operations and sequence-design tasks. These are not 40 confirmed duplicates. |
| ProtocolQA → **ProtocolQA2** | “extends the same approach”: error-injected protocols, with more complex protocols and PDF inputs. [§2.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS4) | **8/125 (6.4%)** reuse underlying protocols from two v1 questions: seven western-blot variants and one plasmid-preparation variant. Different injected errors and answers, but **the same troubleshooting task family**. |
| CloningScenarios → **CloningQA** | No explicit description of overlap. [§2.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS5) | **14/14** share DNA segments ≥100 bases with v1. However, inspection of all 33 v1 and 14 v2 prompts found no obvious identical full scenario. **Substantial planning/output shift:** answer questions about a scenario → construct a complete protocol and reagent designs. |

**New categories:** the paper introduces **PatentQA (121 rows)**, **TrialQA (120 rows)** and **SourceQuality / SourceQualQA (150 rows)** as “new subtask types” ([§2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09554v1#S2.SS1)), with no direct v1 category counterpart. No exact-question, ID or normalized source-identifier matches were found for these categories; semantic examples are included below.

<details>
<summary>Concrete examples behind the semantic assessments</summary>

- **LitQA:** a carryover asks the same relationship between intron and exon methylation, with minor wording changes. Other inspected v2 questions ask for unrelated experimental doses or protein-interaction details.
- **FigQA:** on a shared neuroscience paper, v1 asks which stimulus maximizes a population-distance change; v2 asks what percentage of virgin males responds to social cues. These are different measurements. In the stronger reuse candidate, both versions ask which gene is enriched in both donors during the expansion screen; both answer CRKL. Candidate pair: v1 `69112914-26ca-4430-bd2a-6720d0e03b05` → v2 `dad00259-ca31-41a7-aeba-f8e6e577b1d8`.
- **TableQA:** on the same profilin study, v1 asks which mutation most affects pI; v2 asks the pI of the H120E mutant. In the stronger reuse candidate, both ask for the number of protein-interaction databases in the same review and answer seven. Candidate pair: v1 `6036c219-fd8c-408b-b0e5-a2eaaecbc596` → v2 `a102bad7-90a7-4cc9-a8b9-82665bdc96ca`. Neither figure/table candidate has been confirmed against the original images.
- **SuppQA:** the shared Gene-SGAN row changes from a hyperparameter value to which network component has a bias term. Other examples retrieve primer sequences for different genes or constructs.
- **DbQA:** v1 asks which gene occupies a chromosome band; v2 asks for sequence around a specified gene's transcription start site. V2 also includes expression aggregation, coordinate conversion and structure counts. Shared database names can appear in prompts even when source metadata does not match.
- **SeqQA:** the inspected Gibson pair retains pUC19/SmaI but changes the gene and organism: v1 selects primers, v2 produces them. In one inspected v2 attachment pair, the DNA match came from pUC19, not the supplied genome. New v2 operations include alignment entropy, molecular weight and enzyme kinetics.
- **ProtocolQA:** the shared western-blot protocol tests excess BSA in v1; v2 variants test incubation time, transfer, blocking or detection chemistry. Same experimental workflow, different faults to diagnose.
- **CloningQA:** v1 usually asks about a component or outcome of a supplied scenario, including some protocol-selection questions. V2 asks for complete protocols using Gibson, restriction/ligation or Golden Gate. Familiar techniques transfer, but the required solution is more extensive.
- **PatentQA / TrialQA:** examples ask for patent sequence identifiers and parameter ratios, or trial eligibility thresholds and differences between treatment-arm restrictions. No same-fact v1 counterpart appeared in the inspected candidates.
- **SourceQuality:** reference reasons include nonrandomized study design, the wrong intervention comparison or a missing outcome. We inspected the questions and reference reasons, rather than independently reassessing each paper's scientific eligibility.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Audit scope, inspection coverage and limitations</summary>

**Data:** pinned [v1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench/tree/5c77cec648430f30611808808861eb86f81d5eaa) and [v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/EdisonScientific/labbench2/tree/3678e7e38748477d0606407468db9cd7e2f2e667) revisions. Counts refer to these public revisions and differ from some paper counts. V2 totals include separate figure/table input variants, not 1,912 distinct underlying questions. V1's private holdout was unavailable.

**Automated checks:** IDs, exact and normalized questions, source identifiers, similarity-based candidates, protocol text and exact DNA segments. No identical question strings were found outside LitQA. Figure/table source-overlap counts in the main table use retrieval variants; image and PDF variants each had 30/101 matches for FigQA and 82/100 for TableQA.

**Direct semantic inspection:** all 86 DbQA2 prompts; all 33 v1 and 14 v2 cloning prompts; one example per SeqQA2 template (20), v1 SeqQA template (15) and v1 DbQA template (10); and six deterministically selected rows each from LitQA3, FigQA2, TableQA2, SuppQA2, ProtocolQA2 and the three new categories, alongside candidate v1 matches. We also revisited the identified protocol pairs and figure/table candidates, supplementing the earlier review of the 43 LitQA carryovers. DbQA inspection was not an exhaustive comparison against all 520 v1 rows.

**Limits:** semantic findings describe inspected examples and task families, not a measured percentage of semantic duplicates. Figure/table inspection used retrieval questions and reference answers, without verifying the original images. Source matching does not resolve alternate URLs or missing metadata. DNA checks covered contiguous A/C/G/T strings in v1 question text and supplied v2 sequence files, including reverse complements; they excluded answer/distractor-only sequences, runtime-retrieved inputs and approximate similarity. One v2 protocol PDF yielded no extractable text. The paper gives no category-by-category numerical overlap audit; our measured overlaps should not be attributed to the authors.

</details>

issues.title: [eval] Add no-tools LAB-Bench evaluations with separate component scores

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
Add small structural evals for basic agent behavior. The [BixBench trace audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found answers left in chat instead of the required file, and simulated tool execution with no actual tool calls. The audit does not isolate model behavior from serving, tool parsing, or harness behavior.

Cover four checks:

- Required-file submission: when instructed to write an answer to a path, verify that a nonempty file exists in the actual task environment. An answer in chat or a claimed write does not pass.
- Actual tool execution: verify a real tool invocation and its execution status for tasks that need one. Tool-call markup, invented tool responses, or a narrated shell session do not pass. Distinguish missing/invalid invocations, executor failures/timeouts, and successful execution.
- Thinking disabled: verify the emitted response respects the supported `thinking=false` setting. Define the prohibited reasoning-channel output or delimiters under the pinned template; this checks observable output, not internal reasoning. Keep extraction/serving errors distinguishable from model violations.
- URL loading: when a task explicitly requires information at a supplied URL and a retrieval tool is available, verify an actual retrieval attempt. Record tool/network failures separately from failure to attempt retrieval.

Done when:

- Each check has minimal tasks and positive/negative grader fixtures, including narrated execution and missing-file cases.
- Results separate protocol compliance, submission completeness, and answer correctness. Passing the structural check alone must not imply a correct answer.
- Traces retain the request settings, raw response, parsed tool calls, execution events, and checked artifacts needed to locate failures.

Scope is evaluation additions; training interventions are separate.

Related: #10060 (output-contract validation), #10061 (tool-protocol syntax and localized supervision).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [BixBench audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258#issuecomment-6300963037) found 156/205 tasks without the required answer file and a trace that narrated shell execution with no tool event; the evidence does not isolate model output from parsing or execution. Harbor keeps a trajectory but maps verifier reward to one `correct` value, leaving no separate protocol, submission, and answer labels. The duplicate preflight found no PR for these four checks; [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) covers BFCL training and syntax diagnostics.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial_driver.py#L316-L352`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L316-L352) — validates one Harbor dataset and agent.
- [`runner.py#L126-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L126-L145) — reads trial result and trajectory path.
- [`runner.py#L172-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L172-L189) — equates reward with `correct`.
- [`eval.py#L111-L141`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L111-L141) — sample and metric contract.
- [`eval.py#L288-L342`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py#L288-L342) — flattened trajectory fields.

# Design: agent protocol probes

Add a versioned four-task diagnostic through the evaluation launcher. Pin the model revision, chat template, tool schema/parser, agent/runtime revision, request settings, and task content. Use Harbor's existing local dataset path for sandbox checks; use a dedicated single-turn request to the same served endpoint for `thinking=false`, so the grader can inspect the exact request and response independently of an agent's final message.

1. **Required file.** Ask for a short known answer in `/workspace/answer.txt`. The verifier reads that path in the task environment after the agent stops and records existence, byte count, and content hash. Score file presence separately from matching the known answer; chat text or a claimed write cannot satisfy presence.
2. **Tool execution.** Ask the agent to obtain a per-trial nonce with an exposed shell tool. Record the raw generated response before tool parsing, parsed calls, dispatch/start/end events, and exit status. Label missing or invalid invocation, executor error/timeout, and successful execution separately. A narrated shell session, tool-call markup in ordinary text, or invented tool response must fail the execution check.
3. **Thinking disabled.** Send `enable_thinking=false` only for a pinned template that supports it. Define forbidden reasoning fields and template delimiters for that template; inspect the raw HTTP response and parsed message. An unsupported setting, server error, or extraction failure gets its own status, never a model-violation label. This measures emitted output only.
4. **URL loading.** Supply a task-local HTTP URL serving a per-trial nonce and make a retrieval tool available. Score a request observed by that endpoint or an executor-recorded retrieval attempt. Record no attempt, retrieval/network failure, and successful retrieval separately; compare the answer to the nonce independently. The local endpoint avoids public-site availability as a source of false failures.

Store one versioned evidence bundle per trial with request settings, raw response, parsed calls, execution events, URL access log, and checked file metadata. Archive it alongside the existing raw trajectory through `EvaluationStore`; link it from the sample's grading detail. Export `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness` as distinct numeric metrics; keep `not_evaluable` and its reason in grading detail when a prerequisite failed. Keep `EvalSample.correct` for answer correctness when assessed, and report each rate with its denominator; a structural pass alone cannot raise answer accuracy.

## Validation

Write grader fixtures before implementation. Include positive cases for all four checks: file submission, executed tool call, no emitted reasoning, and successful URL retrieval. Negative cases cover missing and empty files; answer only in chat; a fully narrated fake tool transcript; malformed call; dispatch failure and timeout; URL answer without retrieval and retrieval failure; reasoning-field and delimiter leaks; and a serving/extraction error. Assert both the label and the retained evidence for every fixture. Run the checked-in Harbor config through preflight and one capped end-to-end diagnostic suite covering all four checks on the pinned reference setup before using model comparisons. Keep [#10060](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060) and [#10061](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061) separate: they cover general output contracts and tool-call syntax/training.

## Open question

Do the pinned Pi/Harbor/vLLM versions expose the pre-parser generated text and executor lifecycle? The current archive records parsed tool calls and observations, but does not establish those boundaries. If either is unavailable, add capture there before grading that failure class, and mark earlier traces `not_evaluable`.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The [design comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10393#issuecomment-6302257478) covers the cause: Harbor maps verifier reward to a single `correct`, and ATIF trajectories record parsed tool calls and observations but no executor lifecycle or pre-parser text. No open PR covers these checks.

- [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py) — one reward per trial.
- [`trajectory.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trajectory.py) — the trajectory archive the evidence bundle sits beside.
- [`eval.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ae74d9560/lib/finestore/src/finestore/eval.py) — `EvalSample`, `Grading.detail`, and `EvaluationStore.add_artifact`.

# Proposed Fix

This PR adds the grader layer in `marin.evaluation.protocol_probes`: a versioned evidence bundle, one typed spec and grader per check, the four minimal tasks, archiving that stores the bundle and links it from the sample, and denominator-aware rates for `protocol_compliance`, `submission_completeness`, and `answer_correctness`. Fixtures cover every positive and negative case listed in the design. When a prerequisite is missing, such as no captured executor lifecycle, the result is `not_evaluable` and never a model violation. A follow-up will connect the tasks to Harbor runs and the served endpoint once the capture question is settled.

comments.author: davidlundgren

🤖 #10399 now evaluates the probes in the quick RL loop: `train_quick_loop.py` binds an `rl-data/protocol-probes` artifact (eight tasks per check) as a second validation source, the file and tool probes run on ShellSim through per-dataset `task_spec` settings, and SkyRL reports `eval/protocol-probes/protocol/<check>/<result>` rates with `_assessed` denominators. `GradingAttempt.request_settings` keeps the request options, so traces hold the request settings, raw response, tool calls, execution results and checked files.

comments.author: davidlundgren
comments.body:
🤖 #10399 now derives the checks from the attempt instead of declaring them on the task: a file answer, shell-bound tools, declared fetch pages, and a request that turned thinking off each imply a check, and the assessments land in `GradeResult.diagnostics["protocol"]` keyed by check. TaskSpec is unchanged.

Measured on Iris with Qwen3-0.6B served by vLLM on one H100 (32 probes, ~9 minutes wall, the evaluations themselves seconds):

- The first runs rejected every tool-bearing request with HTTP 400 and recorded no reason. The dump now keeps vLLM's message: `"auto" tool choice requires --enable-auto-tool-choice and --tool-call-parser to be set`. The quick-loop and smoke launchers enable the Hermes parser; the quick loop lacked it before, so any tool-offering task would have been masked the same way.
- With the parser on, all 32 probes grade. Qwen3-0.6B never called a tool: `tool_execution` `no_invocation` 8/8, `url_loading` `not_attempted` 8/8, `required_file` `missing_file` 8/8, all with wrong answers. The thinking check, applied to every row because the launch disables thinking, reported `reasoning_emitted` on 20/32 rows before training.
- Locally on CPU with the same model: `respected` on all rows, `no_invocation` and `not_attempted` on the tool and URL probes.

The smoke and the local command are in the quick-RL-loop recipe.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## STATUS
Sorry guys this is currently all AI-generated. Will clean up as we get further in the experiment.

## TL;DR

**Final, 2026-10-24: stopped and written up.** No SFT method beat plain SFT by enough to matter; the source of the traces decided the result. See the [summary comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213#issuecomment-6618401658) and the [paper](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/ecc87c8c082d7bc98df3120cbbf97d748f8f1cd5/logbooks/10213-sft-shootout/agentic-sft-shootout.pdf). The design-stage text below is kept as written.

Design stage, 2026-10-16. We compare five supervised fine-tuning (SFT) mechanisms for agentic coding on one base, one task pool, one teacher and one supervised-token budget: plain SFT (one accepted demonstration per task), rejection-sampled SFT with resampling across epochs, relay SFT (#10027), recovery SFT, and plateau dropping (#10028). The earlier transfer experiments (#9920, #9984) compared plain SFT, rejection-sampled SFT, on-policy distillation and weight merging on non-agentic tasks; this experiment moves to agentic tasks under the eval policy (#10197) and drops merging and distillation. Nothing has trained yet except a learning-rate sweep of the control, which is in progress.

## Question

Which mechanism, if any, improves Snowball v0 on SWE-bench Verified and the terminal benchmarks over plain SFT at equal supervised tokens, without losing retention on GSM8K, BFCL-Parity and GPQA-Diamond.

## Fixed choices

- Base: Snowball v0 = `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12` @ `4eeb756b`. v0 carries a diluted DARE graft of the allkimi relay SFT, so relay's lift reads smaller than it would on a pre-graft checkpoint; this is accepted because the question is what improves the release.
- Task pool: about 2,200 TMax environments (`allenai/TMax-SFT-16.5K`, tasks.zip) and about 2,100 SWE-smith tasks sampled from the Harbor packages in `DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s`, stratified by repository, SWE-bench Verified repositories removed, decontaminated through DataKit against SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and TBLite 2.0. Selection is outcome-blind. SWE-smith packages receive a git-history strip before the agent phase (#10212).
- Harness per task family, matching the policy's scoring agent: TMax under Terminus-2, SWE-smith under mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, both in Harbor under the policy pins.
- Teacher: GLM 5.3 through the internal inference service, 8 attempts per task, verified by each task's tests. v0 is never sampled except in relay, where it starts each task and GLM continues after a trigger (format error, context budget, completion claim).
- Recipe, shared by every arm: the #9984 comparison-arm settings (AdamW, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, clip 1.0, router bias frozen, batch 16 at 32k context, constant learning rate, loss averaged over supervised tokens), 3 epochs, replay of general SFT data (`nemotron_sft_v3`, reasoning kept) at one quarter of the agentic budget. The learning rate comes from the sweep below.

## Arms and token matching

B is the supervised-token count of the plain arm: the first passing attempt per task with at least one pass, one trajectory per task. Every arm trains on B agentic tokens plus the same replay slice for the same number of optimizer steps.

- Plain SFT (control): as above.
- RS-multi: identical task slots to plain; when a task recurs in a later epoch, a different passing attempt is used. Measures demonstration diversity at a fixed budget.
- Relay (#10027): v0's own turns stay in context with no loss; GLM's turns are trained; passing episodes subsampled to B. Episodes with no teacher turn are dropped.
- Recovery (phase 2): the plain trajectories; 20% receive one or two synthetic failed turns re-rendered in v0's measured error styles plus the real harness error, inserted through the parser; injections carry no loss, so the budget equals B by construction. Waits on a validated injection generator.
- Plateau dropping (#10028, phase 2): the plain trajectories; tokens whose loss has plateaued lose gradient; matched on optimizer steps, with gradient-carrying tokens reported. Waits on the trainer.

Phase 1 is plain, RS-multi and relay.

## Evaluation

Every arm, including plain, runs the retention gate (GSM8K, BFCL-Parity, GPQA-Diamond) and the agentic endpoint (SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1, TBLite 2.0) under the policy's trial counts and pins. An arm passes when it has no decisive loss against plain on the gate and a decisive win over plain on at least one agentic benchmark with no decisive loss on the others, where decisive is the policy's rule (gap above 1.96 times the combined task-level standard error, each scaled by 1/sqrt(0.9)). One policy run resolves gaps of roughly 4 to 5 points on SWE-bench Verified and 8 to 10 on the terminal benchmarks; unresolved arms are reported with intervals and not promoted. Passing arms, plain and v0 go to the 23-benchmark tournament.

## Learning-rate sweep of the control

Running now, on pilot data (existing Qwen3.6-27B TMax traces and Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith traces, history-reading trials removed), four runs from v0 at 3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6 and 1e-5, 3 epochs, recipe otherwise fixed. Screens per run: held-out validation loss on 5% of tasks, GSM8K, BFCL-Parity, SWE-bench Verified random-100 and a 100-task TBLite subset. Decision rule, fixed in advance: among rates with no decisive retention loss against v0, the best equal-weight mean of the two agentic screens; ties to the smaller rate. The chosen rate is confirmed once on the real plain-arm data and then frozen for all arms.

## Budget

Core (sweep, generation, phase 1, tournament) about 3,700 to 4,000 H100-hours; phase 2 adds about 2,400, of which 1,700 is an optional 20-epoch plateau comparison. GLM generation runs on the internal service and sandbox CPU and is outside the GPU budget.

## Status and next steps

- Pilot dataset and learning-rate sweep: in progress.
- Task pool, decontamination and package fix: in progress.
- Harness bring-up, one-task dry runs, a 200-task-per-family pass-rate pilot and a relay dry run: in progress. The full 8-attempt generation waits on their results.
- Then: phase-1 training, first-stage evaluation, tournament for passers; phase 2 when its code exists.

Design notes and diagrams are kept in the maintainer's notes and will be attached as results land.

## Decision log

- 2026-10-15: scope cut to SFT only; merging and on-policy distillation dropped. Base set to Snowball v0.
- 2026-10-16: one harness per task family following the policy's scoring agents; GLM 5.3 as the single teacher with regenerated traces instead of reusing Kimi and Qwen traces; RS arm redefined as resampling across epochs after the token-budgeted variant was found to re-weight tasks; task eligibility defined by teacher success only; unfiltered-SFT control dropped; primary endpoint set to the agentic benchmarks with the tournament secondary; git-history leak found in the SWE-smith packages and a strip added to the pool build.

comments.body:
🤖 Teacher generation bring-up: one-task dry runs

## TL;DR

GLM 5.3 now runs end to end in both harnesses (Harbor `016dd78b`, Daytona sandboxes, run from cw-us-east-02a):
- TMax under Terminus-2, with the 65,536 / 16,384 limits from the policy;
- SWE-smith under the mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 adapter, with a 32,768-token window.

**The adapter question is answered.** The mini-swe-agent adapter runs a raw SWE-smith Harbor package unchanged, and the dry-run trace fit inside 32k (largest prompt 13.4k tokens). One trace says nothing about the length distribution; the pilot will measure it.

**The GLM pass on SWE-smith read the fix from git history** (#10212). Before the SWE-smith pass-rate pilot, the packages need the history-stripped repair.

**The pilot has not started.** It waits on a capacity confirmation for the GLM service.

## Per trial

| | TMax `task_000000_5c5b0938` | SWE-smith `swesmith-00003` |
|---|---|---|
| Reward | 0 in the first run, 1 in a rerun | 1 in both runs |
| Model calls | 4 | 16 to 17 |
| Prompt tokens (total / largest) | 9.3k to 10.1k / 3.7k | 145k to 156k (about 93% prefix-cached) / 13.4k |
| Completion tokens (reasoning) | 5.1k to 6.2k (4.2k to 5.2k) | 3.4k to 3.6k (0.5k to 0.8k) |
| Model time | 39 s | 16 s |
| Trial wall time | 42 to 93 s (environment build 3 to 45 s) | 74 to 80 s (verifier 20 to 25 s) |

## Effective generation settings

Both clients send only `model` and `max_tokens=16384`, so GLM runs on the service defaults. GLM 5.3's template then renders `Reasoning Effort: Max`.

Every request is logged by an in-cluster proxy. The log records the settings as sent and the full reply, reasoning included. The proxy also serves `/tokenize` with the `zai-org/GLM-5.3` tokenizer, because the mini-swe-agent context limiter needs it and the relay does not provide it. Its token counts matched the service on every request.

## Transcripts

Both harnesses write Harbor ATIF trajectories:
- **Terminus-2:** each step's message is the JSON action, and the reasoning is in `reasoning_content`.
- **mini-swe-agent:** native `bash` tool calls with `{returncode, output}` observations, but the trajectory **drops GLM's reasoning**. Training rows are therefore rebuilt from the proxy log, which keeps it. That rebuild checks clean on both dry runs.

## What the agent can see

Measured with an oracle-agent probe during the agent phase:

| | TMax (converted) | SWE-smith (raw package) |
|---|---|---|
| `/tests` | absent | absent |
| `/solution` | absent | absent |
| Other task files | none | none |
| Git history | no repository | 944 branches, including `main` and the full history |

The SWE-smith dry-run pass used that history: it ran `git show 614b134:<file>`, then checked its edit against that file. Details are in #10212.

## Other findings

- **TMax is not in Harbor format** in `tasks.zip`. The pool converts it with TMax's own `convert_to_harbor.py` at `hamishivi/tmax@6d3d606c`, minus 181 environments with hidden verifier assets, giving 2,019 tasks.
- **The dry-run TMax task looks flawed.** It runs an OpenMP parallel loop over the outer LU loop with 4 threads, while the test expects the sequential determinant. The task failed once and passed once.

## Next

- **TMax pilot:** 200 tasks x 2 attempts, seed 20261016, drawn uniformly from 1,963 eligible tasks (the pool minus #202's held-out ids). Staged; starts when capacity is confirmed.
- **SWE-smith pilot:** 200 x 2, stratified by repository, on the history-stripped packages.
- **Relay dry run:** 20 tasks per family, with v0 served by the policy serving config. GLM takes over on these triggers:
  - format error: GLM writes one repair turn;
  - context budget at 0.75 of the window: GLM continues to the end;
  - completion claim: v0's reply is withheld and logged, and GLM continues to the end.

Run folders: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/generation/dryrun/{tmax-dry1,tmax-dry2,swe-dry3,swe-dry4,visibility1}`

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Relay rounds broken by a preempted student server ([#10237](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10237)).

**Affected rounds**
- TMax relay shard-02 round 1: 198 of 200 trials errored, 14:33-15:13 UTC on 2026-10-17. Moved to `traces/tmax-relay/shard-02/round-1.failed-0a6b03ad`; it will be rerun. It was never published.
- SWE-smith relay shard-00 round 3: 85 of 97 trials errored, from about 08:29 UTC. Its 32 valid rows are published; trials that raised without a GLM reply don't count as relay runs.

I'm checking every other round for a student preemption and will post the full list.

**Cause.** In relay mode, the v0 student runs as a child inference job. When that job was preempted, Iris rescheduled it on another host. The relay proxy kept calling the address resolved once at startup (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py:682`). Every student call then failed with `httpx.ConnectError`, the agents got HTTP 500, and Harbor still exited 0.

**Fix** (`task/212` @ [`174906474a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/174906474a8039d1ff8989e8f6d53103242cfec1)):
- On a connection error, the proxy looks up the student's current address and retries for up to 20 minutes.
- The proxy logs its own failures, which used to go unlogged.
- A run fails, with no `_SUCCESS`, when more than 20% of its trials raise without a reply.

The relay lanes are being resubmitted on this commit.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Decisions for the next data round (v7), 2026-10-19.

1. Regenerate the GLM 5.3 pool at a lower reasoning effort. The max-effort traces caused both phase-1 defects: long reasoning used up the 30k generation window (so half of the passing SWE-smith attempts never reached the submit step) and taught a style that times out TBLite. GLM 5.3's chat template exposes only `low`, `high` and max (`medium` renders as max, and `high` reasoned to the token cap like max in a probe), so a pilot of 200 TMax and 200 SWE-smith tasks x 2 samples at `low` and `high` is running (launched 21:01 UTC) to measure pass rate, clean-pass rate, per-turn reasoning and context use against the max-effort pool. The full k=8 regeneration on pool v5, plus relay rounds, follows at the chosen setting with the same gates.
2. Select demonstrations by clean completion: an attempt counts only if it passed and ended with the agent's own finish (mini-swe-agent submit, Terminus-2 `task_complete`). On the max-effort traces this keeps 919 of 1,995 SWE-smith tasks and 1,475 of 1,914 TMax tasks; the lower-effort traces should keep more.
3. Switch the base to Snowball v0.1 (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14`, selected in #10283 under the same policy). Same architecture, tokenizer and template as v0, and without v0's relay SFT graft, so it is a cleaner base for the relay arm. The relay student becomes v0.1 and v0.1 reference screens will be run. The LR sweep result (1e-6, 3 epochs) is carried over rather than repeated.
4. Rebuild all five arms on the new rows, retrain and screen them. The v5 arms above remain the max-effort finding.

Recovery SFT implementation check: the owner obtained the original recovery generation code; the mechanism matches ours (injection points, 1–3 attempts, Terminus-2 reply template and parser, teacher-authored failed turns, masking). Two rendering details from it are adopted (varied renders per error style; streaks of the same style, with rates measured on v0's own trajectories: 56.6% same style, 0% identical); we keep trained tokens equal to plain's.
