GLM read `tenacity/retry.py` from it and called it "the reference". The conda base in the images also holds boltons 23.0.0. All four repos (469 tasks) are excluded from pool P.

**Why not a whole-trial block:** Harbor sets the Daytona network policy once per sandbox. Both the mini-swe-agent install and the SWE-smith verifier (`tests/test.sh`) download uv from github.com releases (`astral.sh/uv/0.7.13/install.sh`), so a whole-trial allow-list without github.com breaks them.

**Mechanism** ([`harbor_agents/trial_agents.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1555295d4d5a233e1bb854c814b927c21889574c/experiments/post_training/sft_shootout/harbor_agents/trial_agents.py), `AgentPhaseNetwork`, branch `task/207` @ `1555295d`): just before the agent's run, the live sandbox is switched to `domain_allow_list=iris.oa.dev` (the proxy host). The run starts once that host resolves, and the task's own policy is restored before the verifier. Each trial writes the applied policy to `agent/agent_network.json`, and the run's `driver_config.json` records it under `agent_network`.

**Measured** (null agent on swesmith-00008, -00698, -00763; HTTPS HEAD from inside the sandbox):

| Target | Before | Agent phase | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `https://github.com/swesmith` | 200 | DNS failure | 200 |
| `api.github.com`, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, `codeload.github.com` | 200 | DNS failure | 200 |
| `https://140.82.112.3/`, `https://140.82.114.4/` (GitHub by IP) | 200 | TLS handshake cut | 200 |
| `https://1.1.1.1/` | 403 | TLS handshake cut | 403 |
| `pypi.org`, `deb.debian.org`, `archive.ubuntu.com`, `www.google.com` | 200 | DNS failure | 200 |

On these unchanged trees the verifier completed afterwards and scored 0, as expected. With GLM (`swe-net2`), 3/3 trials passed under the limit, and all 76 proxy calls returned 200. In one trial GLM ran `pip install pytest ...` and saw `No internet`.

A probe ran mini-swe-agent's real setup on one task from each of the 36 repos (`toolenv2`). It found the same 80 distributions on every image. Only three of them are pool repos: pygments (222 tasks), pandas (196) and tenacity (30). Every conda-based image also ships conda's own `boltons-23.0.0` under `/opt/miniconda3/pkgs`, including the mahmoud/boltons image (21 tasks). The install is now pinned (`mini-swe-agent-2.1.0-constraints.txt`, sha256 `c67d1ee2…`, Python 3.12), so this set cannot drift between the pilot and the full run. SWE-smith ingestion also drops any trace whose commands or outputs touch `/root/.local/share/uv/tools/`.

**Run folders** (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/generation/dryrun/`):
- `netprobe2`, `netprobe3`, `netprobe4`: network probes; `agent/network_probe.json` per trial.

comments.author: Min-Li
comments.body:
Data point for Open-SWE, which is in the 10-05 SFT mix but not in the list above. I checked the successful traces (`resolved == 1`) of the two pinned Qwen3.8-27B mini-swe-agent partitions of `nvidia/Open-SWE-Traces` (revision `f967cba3`, 49,925 traces) for lines of the fix that show up in command output before the agent writes them.

**Rule.** A trace is flagged when at least 3 lines added by the reference patch (30+ characters, not imports or comments, not in the removed lines or the prompt) first appear in the output of a command that reads git history (`git log/show/diff`), `site-packages`, `node_modules`, `build/`, `dist/` or `.egg-info`, or the network (`curl`, `wget`, `pip download`, URLs), before the agent writes them. I then read 5 flagged traces per channel.

| Channel | Flagged | Read | Confirmed leak |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| git history | 153 | 5 | 0 |
| `site-packages` | 104 | 5 | 3 |
| `node_modules` | 83 | 5 | 0 |
| other (`build/lib`, network, …) | 29 | 5 | 1 |

- **Git history:** no case like the SWE-smith one. The git hits I read were the agent's own checkout or edits, or an older commit unrelated to the fix.
- **A newer release of the task's own package is installed in the image.** This is a different path from the mini-swe-agent tool env above: the system `site-packages` (`/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages`) holds a newer release of the package being fixed, and that release already contains the fix. For example, the task repo is `mkdocs-include-markdown-plugin` `2.8.0` while `3.4.1` is installed; the other two are `pytest-snapshot` `0.6.3` and `trie` `1.4.0` (which already has the `get_proof` the task asks for). The fourth case is a stale `build/lib/` copy inside the repo (oauthenticator). In all four, the agent found the copy (for example, diffed it against `/testbed`) and said it would not copy it; I did not check whether it used it anyway.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Fuzzy verification in PR #8114 filters a broad set of duplicate candidates after connected-component clustering. This experiment measures whether removed documents are duplicates, whether retained candidates are missed duplicates or distinct documents, and whether the containment and unique-trigram limits should change. A small canary suggests that the current rules are precise but conservative. The 4K smoke and full-text review are in progress.

## Description

The audit reads full text from the CoreWeave source data and writes private reports to GCS. It samples removed, retained, boundary, random, source, length, score, and cluster-size strata. Corpus text stays in private artifacts.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Review at least 500 complete document comparisons, measure the quality of current decisions, test counterfactual parameter settings, and recommend either the current verifier or a measured parameter change. Run matched and larger samples after the 4K output passes its integrity checks.

## Status

The current 4K smoke contains 2,783 candidate clusters and 5,628 documents from 3,998 source shards. It uses 128 shuffle partitions and 32 workers. At 2026-08-11 18:44 UTC, stage 0 was complete and the verification stage was at 2/128 tasks. All 32 workers were alive after 14 preemptions, with no application error.

The exploratory canary has 47 reviewed candidate decisions:

- The current rules removed 4 candidates. All 4 appeared safe to remove.
- The rules retained 43 candidates. Manual review marked 28 as safe removal opportunities and 15 as unsafe to remove.
- The current rules found 4 of the 32 reviewed safe removal opportunities.
- A counterfactual containment limit of 0.90 with 8 unique trigrams found 7 safe removals and no unsafe removal. Limits of 0.85/8 and 0.80/8 found more safe removals but also 1 and 2 unsafe removals, respectively.

The canary is small and selected for inspection, so it does not support a production parameter change by itself. The production defaults have not changed.

A separate stress set contains 1,018 hard pairs from issue #6854. The current rule accepted three pairs, and all three were safe removals. A much smaller relaxation to 0.99 containment with 2 unique trigrams added 20 removals; directional review marked 16 safe and 4 unsafe because they lost a schedule month, a quote ending, an attribution, or a signature. This stress result is evidence against a global threshold reduction, including the canary-fitted 0.90/8 setting.

## Links

* Logbook: will be linked when the research branch is published
* W&B Report: none
* Important updates:
  * [PR #8114](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8114)
  * [4K V6 smoke](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Ffuzzy-verification-audit-4k-v6-20260811)

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-11: Bound the smoke shuffle at 128 partitions after an unbounded run created 3,998 downstream verification tasks.
- 2026-08-11: Set the smoke store-ready and recovery limits to 7,200 seconds after a 1,800-second deadline expired during worker recovery. This did not change production defaults.
- 2026-08-11: Defer parameter changes until the 4K integrity checks, stratified review, matched treatment, and larger samples are complete.

## Conclusion

Open. The final report requires at least three days of analysis and at least 500 complete document comparisons.

comments.body:

- A blind second pass changed two of 155 rejected-comparison labels from safe to information-loss risk. The two SFT records share a prompt and final answer, but contain different generated derivations. Corrected totals are 76 safe misses, 65 information-loss risks, and 14 survivor-quality risks. No threshold replay selects these two records, so the parameter recommendation is unchanged.
- An exact replay compared three survivor policies on the complete inspections. The hashed output has 836 documents and 470,211 whitespace tokens. Keeping both sides of the two primary base-to-derived transformations adds 137 documents and 40,566 tokens, or 8.63%. Preferring the base side adds three documents and removes 11,628 tokens, or 2.47%.
- The 137 hashed matches point to 135 unique derived representatives. Manual review labels 26 representatives as worse and 109 as equal or better. A prefer-base policy removes all 26 worse records, but it also removes added information from 109 quality-safe derived records. A keep-both policy restores the base records but keeps the worse derived records.
- The compact 4K replay gives the same policy shape. Keep-both adds 12.34% of output tokens. Prefer-base removes 3.43% of output tokens.
- The large-cluster replay found two safe recall misses among 439 documents. A 32-record anchor head finds one base-to-question-answer match that the current 64-record head and full-cluster longest anchor miss. Raising the local-representative limit from 64 to 128 finds one format-only capitalization duplicate. This tail contains duplicate subgroups, so full-cluster longest selection is not an exhaustive rule.
- Two comparisons per document remain supported. Across the 4K, hashed, and large-cluster inspections, one comparison loses three removals and saves 562 comparisons. Four comparisons add 571 comparisons and no removals. Eight comparisons add 999 comparisons and no removals.

Decision: Keep the strict containment, local-similarity, and longer-member rules. Keep two comparisons per document. Treat survivor choice as source policy, not threshold tuning. comments.body:
🤖 PR reconciliation found four items to resolve before merge:

- The multiple-canonical invariant has a missed path. Two same-ID, same-text records with two canonical flags are accepted because the representative-ID branch increments `canonicals_seen` and skips the `> 1` check. The current producer's source-prefixed CC IDs should prevent this state in a valid artifact, so this is a failed defensive invariant rather than an observed data error. Add the check and a same-ID regression test.
- The PR body says that each cluster uses its longest document, reaches the exhaustive ceiling, and needs no duplicate subgroups. The implementation selects the longest document only from the first 64 records or 2 million characters. Large-cluster replay found a safe duplicate subgroup that the current primary anchor missed. Narrow these claims to the measured sample.
- Update stale descriptions in `experiments/datakit/README.md`, `fuzzy_dups.py`, and the verifier test comment. Add a behavior test with more than 64 cluster records.
- Make the 64-record and 2-million-character anchor bounds explicit persisted configuration. They affect decisions but are absent from `VerifiedFuzzyDupsAttrData` and the verification step's `hash_attrs`.

The exact anchor-scan replay shows why a larger bound is not a direct fix. On clusters of size 22, 138, and 279, the current 64-record scan accepts 0 documents in 762 comparisons. A 32-record scan accepts 1 safe base-to-question-answer match in 761 comparisons. Scans of 128, 256, and the full cluster accept 0 in 764 comparisons because they select another anchor. Anchor recall is non-monotonic. A separate 128-local-representative replay finds one further safe capitalization-only duplicate that the current 64-representative limit misses.

The comparison-cap sweep does support the current value of 2 on the measured 4K, hashed, and large-cluster inputs:

- cap 1: 1,429 accepted, 3,911 comparisons
- cap 2: 1,432 accepted, 4,473 comparisons
- cap 4: 1,432 accepted, 5,044 comparisons
- cap 8: 1,432 accepted, 5,472 comparisons

Thus, 2 is the first measured recall-saturation point. This replay measures exact decisions and comparison count; it does not provide CPU or RSS measurements for each cap.

Keep the present containment, local-similarity, two-comparison, and 64-representative defaults for this PR. Track two measured follow-ups separately: exact normalized containment recovered all 12 reviewed under-tokenized code copies, and source-aware survivor policy is needed if the desired output must preserve base-source weight. The hashed survivor census preserved information in all 171 removals but kept a worse derived document in 33 cases; keeping both sides of the two main transformations costs 8.63% more output tokens.

comments.body:
🤖 Medium cross-source audit result

- The production-priority v6e job succeeded in 15 minutes 23 seconds with no task failures or root-task preemptions. It inspected 54 clusters and 410 complete documents. Verification evaluated 356 candidates in 589 comparisons, accepted 36, and retained 320.
- Manual review of all 36 accepted cases found that every removal preserves the removed text. Thirty-five removed documents are exact substrings after whitespace and case normalization. The last differs only because the retained page has one additional login option.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
`_select_duplicates` discards the first record of each id group and emits only the rest, so `_write_shard` writes `{id, dup_doc: True}` for each duplicate and nothing for the occurrence that survives (experiments/datakit/global_exact_dedup.py:150, experiments/datakit/global_exact_dedup.py:160). The attributes are sparse by design: on the full 292-source run only 59 sources produced any attribute directory. Nothing in the output records where a flagged duplicate's canonical lives.

Tracing one flagged id therefore costs a scan. Establishing that the four duplicates in `cp/uk_hansard` were cross-source required reading the `id` column of all 11 files in that source, and naming the source that holds each canonical requires a further full pass per candidate source, over sources that can hold thousands of files. The canonical is already well defined at the point it is dropped: the lowest `(file_idx, row_index)` over sources sorted by name, which the reducer holds when it calls `next(records)`.

Done when:
- each duplicate row carries the canonical's location, as the global `file_idx` and `row_index` or the equivalent source tag plus file and row index
- a flagged duplicate can be traced to its canonical without scanning a source
- consumers of the current `{id, dup_doc}` schema either keep working or are updated together with the schema

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

On the `moe_hero_fsdp` GB200 config, `token_embed` **and both of its Adam moments** are fully replicated on every device. That is **8.81 GiB per GPU — 89% of the entire per-device train state (9.87 GiB)** — for a parameter that is 2.94 GiB.

Replicating the *parameter* is deliberate and documented (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/model.py:61-64`):

```python
# The embedding is fully replicated for a local lookup. The language-model head
# is replicated across racks and FSDP-sharded within each rack.
_EMBED_PARTITION_SPEC = P(None, None)
_LM_HEAD_PARTITION_SPEC = P("data", "model")
```

**The optimizer moments inheriting that spec looks unintended.** The locality argument justifies replicating the weight — `_embedding_gather` (`model.py:95`) does a local lookup with no collective. It does not justify replicating `mu` and `nu`, which are touched only by the optimizer update and never gathered per token.

## Measurement

Instrumented dump of the initialized train state, 1 rack (64 GPUs), `d6144 / E128 top-4 / vocab 128256`, `num_layers=1` (minimal-repro config from #7344), `offload_opt_state=True`:

```
[statemem] leaves=90 per_device_total=9.87 GiB global_total=73.22 GiB ratio=7.4x

dev=2.936 GiB glob=2.936 GiB .params.token_embed                                    spec=P(None, None)
dev=2.936 GiB glob=2.936 GiB .opt_state...inner_states['adam'].inner_state[0].mu.token_embed  spec=P(None, None)
dev=2.936 GiB glob=2.936 GiB .opt_state...inner_states['adam'].inner_state[0].nu.token_embed  spec=P(None, None)
```

For contrast, `output_proj` — the same 128256 × 6144 shape — is sharded and costs 64× less per device:

```
dev=0.046 GiB glob=2.936 GiB .params.output_proj                                    spec=P('data', 'model')
dev=0.046 GiB glob=2.936 GiB .opt_state...inner_states['adamh'].inner_state[0].mu.output_proj
dev=0.046 GiB glob=2.936 GiB .opt_state...inner_states['adamh'].inner_state[0].nu.output_proj
```

So the LM head and the embedding are the same size, and one costs 0.14 GiB/device across param+moments while the other costs 8.81 GiB.

## Why it matters now

Sharding `mu`/`nu` over `data` (64-way) while leaving the weight replicated would recover **~5.8 GiB per GPU** and leave the lookup path untouched.

That is not a rounding error on this config. In #7344 we are chasing allocation failures on GPUs reporting **~18 GiB free of 186 GiB**, where a large transient fails with `cuMemAllocAsync ... CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY`. 5.8 GiB is roughly a third of the remaining headroom. It is not the root cause there — the failing allocation is a step transient, not persistent state — but it is a third of the margin the run has to absorb one.

## Suggested fix

Give the embedding's optimizer state its own spec rather than inheriting `_EMBED_PARTITION_SPEC`, e.g. shard `mu`/`nu` on `P("data", None)`. Worth checking whether the MuonH/AdamH grouping (`inner_states['adam']` vs `['adamh']` vs `['muonh']`) makes this a per-group setting.

Two things to verify before/after:
- the embedding update is numerically unchanged (moments are elementwise; sharding them should be a pure placement change),
- no new collective appears in the update — if resharding the moments introduces an all-gather per step, the trade may not be worth it.

## Repro

The dump comes from a small instrumentation helper that walks `jax.tree_util.tree_leaves_with_path(state)` and reports `sharding.shard_shape(...)`-derived per-device bytes per leaf. Happy to upstream it behind a flag if useful — `GrugTrainerConfig.sharding_dump_path` already writes a sharding artifact, but it records specs without sizes, so the cost of a replicated leaf is not visible from it.

🤖 Filed while investigating #7344.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Correction: the HBM figures above are conditional on `offload_opt_state=False`

I need to correct the headline number in this issue. The measurement was real but I
mislabelled what it measures.

**The probe reports logical sharded bytes, not HBM residency.** It walks
`tree_leaves_with_path(state)` and derives per-device bytes from `sharding.shard_shape()` —
it never reads `memory_kind`.

Under the hero default `offload_opt_state=True`, the optimizer moments are placed on
`pinned_host` at initialization and copied device-ward per step immediately before
`optimizer.update`, then returned to pinned host
(`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py:557` and `:637`).

So of the three replicated 2.936 GiB `token_embed` leaves I reported, **only the parameter
is HBM-resident in the steady state**; the two moments are host-resident between steps.

Corrected claim:

- ❌ "8.81 GiB per GPU — 89% of the per-device train state — with ~5.8 GiB recoverable" as a
  statement about **default** HBM. That figure holds only for `offload_opt_state=False`, or
  transiently during the optimizer update.
- ✅ The **logical replication is real**: `token_embed` and both moments are `P(None, None)`
  while the identically-shaped `output_proj` is `P("data", "model")`, a 64× per-device
  difference in the sharded case.

I also want to flag a cost I understated: sharding the moments while keeping the weight
replicated is **not free**. The optimizer would then need an explicit sharded-update or
re-replication strategy, or moment communication. That trade needs measuring, not assuming.

This remains a worthwhile independent memory optimization — it is simply **not** evidence
for #7344, and I should not have leaned on it there. The connection I drew to allocation
headroom in that issue is withdrawn.

Thanks to an independent review pass for catching the `memory_kind` omission.

spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary This issue defines the repeatable GB200 inference benchmark used to evaluate GrugMoE architecture choices before the hero pretraining run. It fixes the validation anchor, hardware, closed-loop rollout workload, plateau throughput metric, repeat rules, and artifact gates so architecture comparisons change one model property or declared bundle at a time. Experiment 0 validated the rolling benchmark with R3 on, but also showed the frozen experiment R3 carrier is expensive: 302.5347 generated tok/s/GPU with R3 off versus 225.6882 with R3 on (-25.40%). The primary architecture matrix should therefore run with R3 off, while production-like chat R3 is measured separately on the reference, payload-changing candidates, and finalists. The companion tracker #7913 is the execution checklist; this issue is the protocol. ### Helpful links - [Companion architecture tracker #7913](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7913) - [Experiment 0 R3 protocol update](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7912#issuecomment-5185894476) - [Reviewed preflight findings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12b4a6f0d8a1ef1e4021e1fa5b0ba0893fb087ed/notes/preflight/findings.md) - [Merged validation-anchor PR #7820](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7820) > [!IMPORTANT] > This issue freezes the inference benchmark, not the pretraining architecture. > The modeling team still owns quality constraints, exact candidate configs, > and the final model. Lower precision, other inference engines, general vLLM > tuning, and speculative decoding are out of scope. ## Benchmark at a glance | Item | Fixed rule | | --- | --- | | Hardware | Four `gb200-4x` nodes: 16 GB200 GPUs in one NVLink domain | | Primary topology | `PP1 TP1 DP16 EP16`; only the topology experiment varies it | | Model | The tracker's exact `d6144`, 48-layer, top-4-of-128 validation anchor | | Stack | Marin's vLLM fork; prefix caching, chunked prefill, CUDA graphs, sampled-token logprob, fixed output length, ignore EOS, and separate R3 routed-expert controls | | Weights / precision | Seeded vLLM dummy weights; BF16 weights and KV cache | | Comparison | Change one model property or declared bundle; keep the commits, flags, workload, seed, routing fixture, and measurement code fixed within the pair | | Headline | Generated tokens/s/GPU during an unprofiled stable plateau | | Material change | At least 5%, with paired repeats agreeing and the delta larger than paired variation | ## Workload Use a rolling, closed-loop queue. A completed request is replaced immediately, which matches saturated rollout generation better than an external-arrival server benchmark. | Cohort | Cached history | User/tool append | Generate | Final context | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Short | 10,240 | 1,024 | 2,048 | 13,312 | | Medium | 30,720 | 1,024 | 2,048 | 33,792 | | Long | 62,464 | 1,024 | 2,048 | 65,536 | Give each cohort one third of the live slots. For the reference, attention/KV finalists, any memory-cliff candidate, and the final model, also run four sequential 2,048-token response turns per branch. Carry each answer into the next prefix. This produces 8,192 generated tokens and final contexts of 22,528, 43,008, and 65,536 tokens. Run a separate one-turn 131K capacity stress for the reference and attention/KV finalists. Preserve earlier thinking blocks in the append-only history by default. If the post-training renderer strips them, freeze that behavior instead and recalibrate the reference. Do not benchmark both policies in the main matrix. ## Run and repeat rules 1. Calibrate concurrency and `max_num_batched_tokens` once on the R3-off reference. Choose the lowest concurrency within 5% of the best observed point, then freeze all runtime flags. Recalibrate only for the topology comparison. 2. Before any architecture comparison, pass two identical rolling R3-off reference arms. Measure R3 separately on the reference using the production-like chat contract and on candidates that change payload shape or transport behavior. The A/A arms must differ by at most 2% and show normal health. 3. Each ordinary arm must include at least 120 plateau seconds, 250,000 generated tokens, and one full workload-manifest pass. All three floors must pass. 4. Compare candidates as A/B and B/A in separate same-allocation pairs. Add a third pair only if the first two disagree, straddle 5%, or show abnormal health. 5. Confirm a decision-driving irreversible choice once on a fresh allocation. 6. Collect headline throughput without a profiler. Profile only an unexplained regression of at least 5%, a missing expected gain, or a health anomaly. If the two-minute A/A fails, extend both arms to five minutes, then ten minutes only if needed. A candidate may receive one labeled tuned diagnostic after a cliff or surprising result; it never replaces the fixed-setting result. ## Valid result gate A result is valid only when all applicable checks pass: - [ ] In-flight requests stay at or above 95% of target concurrency throughout the measured plateau; ramp and drain are excluded. - [ ] Every request succeeds, every required branch completes, and client and engine token totals reconcile. - [ ] The primary comparison has zero KV preemptions and no unlisted setting change. - [ ] When R3 is enabled, it contains every expected token/layer/top-K expert ID with correct alignment. - [ ] MoE-geometry and EP-topology pairs include both canonical dummy routing and one deterministic balanced-routing control. - [ ] Any new hot-path implementation family has one no-op throughput control. - [ ] Exact configs, train-to-serve parity, commits, image, placement, workload, and artifact readback are recorded. Serving must compute every selected top-K expert contribution with the frozen QB bias. No inference capacity factor may drop assignments. ## Execution checklist - [ ] Modeling acknowledges the validation anchor and marks every live P1 candidate **Include** or **Exclude**, supplying one complete config for each included candidate. - [ ] Check whether vLLM's closed-loop dispatcher accepts the frozen workload. Reuse it when it does; otherwise port only its scheduling and steady-window logic into the existing preflight harness. - [ ] Freeze clean, pushed Marin and Marin-vLLM commits, image, flags, workload, history policy, R3 carrier, route fixture, and artifact schema. - [ ] Use the preflight's zero-retry unattended Iris gang path for calibration, A/A, and candidate pairs. - [ ] Pass the rolling R3-off A/A gate and the separate reference production-like chat-R3 measurement. - [ ] Run the companion tracker's order and attach one valid result packet to each completed row. - [ ] Share the inference recommendation with modeling before architecture freeze. Keep experimental code on long-lived Marin and Marin-vLLM branches. Open a PR only for code with a clear reusable consumer or for the selected production model path.
Exact load generation and plateau calculation Use six frozen roots per cohort and eight rollout branches per root. A completion is replaced by the next request from that cohort's frozen root/branch schedule, with no think time. Keep each root and its branches on one DP rank. Freeze and hash token IDs, root and branch order, turns, sampling parameters, and per-request seeds. Warm with disjoint requests, reset the prefix cache, then populate histories through normal server requests. For the four-turn trajectory, use these exact initial histories: | Cohort | Initial history | Total generated | Final context | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Short | 10,240 | 8,192 | 22,528 | | Medium | 30,720 | 8,192 | 43,008 | | Long | 53,248 | 8,192 | 65,536 | The separate 131K stress uses 121,856 cached tokens, a 1,024-token append, an 8,192-token response, and `max_model_len=131072`. Open the plateau when in-flight requests reach `ceil(0.95 × target_concurrency)`. If any sample falls below that threshold, discard the window and reopen it after recovery. Close the plateau while the queue is still full, after all duration, token, and manifest floors pass. Then stop refilling and exclude the drain. ```text generated tokens/s/GPU = sum of unique vLLM generation-counter deltas during the plateau / plateau seconds / serving GPUs ``` Use generation-counter snapshots at plateau boundaries. Do not reconstruct plateau throughput from completed requests. After drain, cross-check the whole-run counter delta against successful-request token totals. The smaller-local-KV stretch may use only 8,192- and 65,536-token final contexts, with the same append and generation lengths. Add no midpoint or 131K arm to that first screen.
Routing, R3, profiling, and implementation controls Record per-expert and contiguous EP-rank assignment histograms for every arm. Canonical dummy routing is primary. Because preflight found it highly skewed, repeat MoE-geometry and EP-topology pairs with one deterministic balanced runtime route. Use that control elsewhere only when a decision-relevant delta coincides with different route loads. Do not add skew or capacity-factor sweeps. Pin the vLLM commit and R3 carrier. Run the primary architecture matrix with R3 off. At the reference point, report the production-like chat-R3 throughput delta, payload bytes, and transport time. Add R3-on controls for candidates that change payload dimensions or transport behavior, and for decision-driving finalists; its cost need not be linear across architectures. For a new hot path, compare the implementation enabled versus a no-op path once at the reference configuration. Profile a triggered anomaly for only a few seconds at the same saturated point and link it to the unprofiled result.
Metrics and saved artifacts Each result reports: | Group | Required fields | | --- | --- | | Throughput | Generated and processed-prompt tok/s/GPU; paired delta; plateau seconds and generated tokens | | Load / latency | Target and min/mean/max in-flight; successes/failures; cohort completions; server p50/p99 TTFT and TPOT; client end-to-end latency | | KV / scheduler | Predicted semantic KV bytes; active bytes/live sequence; reserved and peak pool bytes; resident sequences/DP rank; prefix-hit ratio; running/waiting requests; preemptions | | MoE / R3 | Per-expert and per-rank assignments; max/mean rank load; route fixture; carrier; payload bytes; transport time; ID alignment | | Reproduction | Immutable Marin and vLLM URLs; image digest; lock; flags; workload hash/seed; Iris job; task count; NVLink domain; artifact prefix | Keep predicted semantic KV bytes, physically active pages, and the reserved reusable pool separate. Explain an active-versus-predicted gap above 10%. Store each run under: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/inference-bench/grugmoe-architecture///` ```text manifest.json events.jsonl metrics/raw-*.prom metrics/map.json result.json result.md profiles/ # diagnostic runs only ``` The manifest includes code, image, dependency, config, workload, job, placement, flags, R3, and final-prefix provenance. A separate authorized task must read every claimed object, verify hashes and aggregates, and exit successfully.
What preflight proved—and did not prove The [reviewed preflight](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12b4a6f0d8a1ef1e4021e1fa5b0ba0893fb087ed/notes/preflight/findings.md) proved that the exact anchor starts and generates on four `gb200-4x` nodes with `PP1 TP1 DP16 EP16`. Exact-path parity, prefix reuse, active-KV accounting, P0 implementation smokes, unattended launch, and independent artifact readback passed. Its drained-wave A/A arms produced 1,578.25 and 1,583.50 aggregate generated tok/s, a 0.3324% difference, with zero preemptions. This proves feasibility and drained-wave repeatability. It does not pass the rolling A/A gate or rank an architecture. The dummy router left 121 of 128 experts unused, and the bounded Snowball attempt failed before model load, so this is not trained-model performance evidence. | Provenance | Frozen value | | --- | --- | | Live Marin / vLLM | [`a3320a3`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/a3320a3043018ee923bc98bf2e6e6eef3f03a6fe) / [`2c2bef3`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/2c2bef33dfbd7aef3c9d4433a7e4110f77d56a4a) | | Reviewed heads | [`12b4a6f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/12b4a6f0d8a1ef1e4021e1fa5b0ba0893fb087ed) / [`73b6fc9`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/73b6fc9cc20c2712ec8798dd017d8a5bc9f55b5b) | | Image | `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:5e2a69af91a000cb999e6ff0d92933874bd3142eb45469fc64fc7a3f5db64fbb` | | Placement | Four whole GB200 nodes in `DH1-129-US-EAST-08A`; `PP1 TP1 DP16 EP16` |
References - [#7201: GB200 architecture TPS tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201) - [#7673: provisional pretraining and RL timelines](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7673) - [#7706: serving topology study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7706) - [#7164: train-to-serve routing parity](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7164) - [#7248: R3 payload and transport measurements](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7248) - [#7820: exact merged GrugMoE reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7820)

spillover_issues.body:
Follow-up to #7878 and part of #7786.

The pinned three-arm eight-H100 gate did not pass: rank topology differed, expert routes differed on every rank, and 46 of 1,296 sampled gradient values exceeded tolerance. Outputs, loss, finiteness, the shared timing seam, and eager instrumentation passed. Per the stop rule, no 32-H100 timing run was submitted.

## Next step

Run a bounded same-process, same-input layer sweep and identify the first routed block where hidden values, top-k routes, or backward gradients diverge. Keep the diagnostic focused; do not build a new general benchmark harness.

comments.body:
🤖 The smallest supported combine correction has now been tested through the
frozen production gate. It fixes the fixed-route BF16 accumulation discrepancy,
but it does not pass live-routing acceptance. I am therefore keeping the local
candidate out of MarinSkyRL #276 and leaving this issue open with the remaining
boundary stated explicitly.

## What was localized and tried

At #276 head `0c213586b5491b8046ca7780e965c4b26dc6a2a2`, the real grouped expert
output agreed with an independent slot-wise reference before combination. The
first fixed-route mismatch appeared when weighted BF16 expert outputs were
combined with `index_add_`; eager and grouped used different BF16 accumulation
orders.

Local-only candidate `fbb1fc8378601e0346d00d186809f10d1ad0360d`
(`12` changed production lines: 6 added and 6 removed, plus one focused
regression) accumulated the already BF16 weighted contributions in FP32 in both
paths, then cast the combined result back to the model dtype. It did not change
routing, expert computation, or the BF16 multiplication. With that candidate,
eager, grouped, and the independent FP32 slot-wise reference were bitwise equal
in the one-H100 fixed-route test; combine-weight, gate, up, and down gradients
were bitwise equal, and hidden gradients were within the frozen bound.

The ordinary local commands were:

```text
cd skyrl-train
.venv/bin/ruff check skyrl_train/models/grug_moe.py tests/cpu/models/test_grug_moe.py tests/gpu/diag_grug_grouped_combine.py
.venv/bin/pytest -q tests/cpu/models/test_grug_moe.py -k 'bfloat16_expert_combine or native_grouped_mm_builds'
.venv/bin/pytest -q tests/cpu/models/test_grug_moe.py
.venv/bin/pytest -q tests/cpu/models/test_grug_model_wrapper.py tests/cpu/test_trainer.py
.venv/bin/pytest --collect-only -q tests/gpu/test_grug_fsdp2_rl_cycle.py tests/gpu/diag_grug_grouped_combine.py
cd ..
uv run infra/pre-commit.py --changed-files --fix
uv run infra/pre-commit.py --review
```

Results were `2 passed`, `19 passed`, `32 passed`, the two intended GPU tests
collected, Ruff passed, the changed-file gate passed, and the post-commit review
had no candidate-specific finding. The candidate contains only the model change
and CPU regression; `tests/gpu/diag_grug_grouped_combine.py` is an unpushed,
evidence-only diagnostic.

## Frozen 8-H100 fixed-replay preflight: pass

[Writer job](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fromain%2Fgrug-paired-preflight-fbb1fc8-s1-r4-20260803)
and [out-of-process artifact reader](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fromain%2Fgrug-candidate-preflight-readback-fbb1fc8-s1-20260803)
used one H100x8 node, the pinned image and replay, retained live-route
capture/compare, and three restored arms. Each arm computed its own routes; the
harness did not force expert IDs or weights.

- `preflight_valid=true`; every identity, topology, state, RNG, path,
  allocation, and finiteness check passed.
- Grouped versus eager: action log probabilities `0/24` violations; CE exact;
  gradients `0/1,296` violations, maximum absolute difference
  `0.009979724884033203`, maximum allowance ratio `0.7054788573413215`.
- Route readback covered 208 rank-layers, 1,666,496 tokens, and 6,665,984
  routed allocations, with zero route changes or ordered-slot mismatches.
- This preflight sampled only 24 action log probabilities. It is a prerequisite,
  not a substitute for the 12,288-sample production gate below.
- Artifact:
  `s3://marin-us-east-02a/iris/grug-training-perf-gap/20260803/divergence-closeout-fbb1fc8/preflight-paired-s1.json`
  (payload SHA-256
  `c5039fccf7b2988afd66020be40a828faac0b84a69dc387895df0532036eddb2`,
  result SHA-256
  `4f0534bbb19fe577a8c3c5b9876b555bb183f7499922c4606bb2b4731250c878`).

## Sole frozen 32-H100 live-routing pair: fail

An identical East submission never started a task and was stopped before the
approved RNO replacement. The RNO job below is the sole executed full pair.

One [production-priority writer pair](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fromain%2Fgrug-paired-eager-grouped-fbb1fc8-s1-rno-20260803)
ran eager then grouped on the same four H100x8 nodes, using the same replay,
model state, RNG restoration, topology, and timing boundary. It used 24 CPU and
1,200 GiB of RAM per replica, with zero retries. The
[CPU-only out-of-process artifact reader](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fromain%2Fgrug-candidate-headline-readback-fbb1fc8-s1-20260803)
rehashes the artifact, checks every pin, and recomputes the comparisons. It
detects pin drift, corruption, and disagreement with the embedded verdict; it
uses the same frozen comparison formulas, so it is not an independent numerical
oracle for those formulas.

- Structural, identity, state, path, finiteness, HBM-fit, and preflight
  prerequisite checks passed.
- CE passed: eager `2.0137084914302568`, grouped `2.013707667627426`, absolute
  difference `8.238028308404921e-7`, zero violations.
- Representative gradients passed: `0/5,184` violations, maximum absolute
  difference `8.058547973632812e-5`, maximum allowance ratio
  `0.04737719830200122` under `rtol=8e-2, atol=1e-4`.
- Representative action log probabilities failed the frozen
  `rtol=4e-2, atol=4e-3` rule: `3/12,288` violations, maximum absolute
  difference `0.1936483383178711`, maximum allowance ratio
  `1.2135916499343056`.
- Therefore `semantic_pass=false`, `correctness_pass=false`, and the candidate
  is rejected.

The reader recomputes the representative-gradient comparison separately rather
than including it in its `semantic_pass` boolean. The gradient check passed, so
that frozen-reader definition does not change the rejection caused by action
outputs.

Artifact:
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/iris/grug-training-perf-gap/20260803/divergence-closeout-fbb1fc8/headline-paired-s1.json`
(payload SHA-256
`f06f4d21722e23843758537f72f79c52d3ebb54120b7344ac1f2d622dcdf5546`,
result SHA-256
`2bf1c1b9ec35ea37adb2180eae51988b49c19e2e34171188f012cdc9219af8e2`).

The observed synchronized walls were `7692.212712150998` seconds eager and
`540.6415278580971` seconds grouped, a ratio of `14.22793536158026`. This is
diagnostic timing only, not an accepted speedup claim, because the same artifact
failed semantics. The old `18.811970x` observation remains invalid as well.

Peak host memory was 69.7--73.7 GB per 1,200-GiB replica. Swap use and every
cgroup OOM counter stayed zero. Peak allocated HBM was 40,599,964,672 bytes
eager and 38,400,473,600 bytes grouped; both arms reserved at most
51,143,245,824 bytes. After the result was durable and GPU processes had exited,
the four containers remained in idle Ray cleanup and were stopped to release
the reservation. No GPU rerun was submitted. The out-of-process reader
intentionally has terminal state `failed` because the frozen gate was false.

## Diagnosis and disposition

This establishes two separate facts:

1. BF16 combine accumulation order was the fixed-route mismatch, and FP32
   accumulation removes that mismatch.
2. That correction is insufficient for the full live-routing workload. The
   production arms still exceed the accepted action-output tolerance.

The headline artifact did not retain paired per-token route traces. It therefore
does not prove that a specific router operation, route flip, grouped GEMM shape,
or later numerical effect caused the three remaining failures. I am not using
the earlier route-margin predicate to waive them. No second small correction is
supported by the frozen evidence; forcing eager reduction order would erase the
grouped implementation rather than minimally repair it, and full Grug R3 or a
memory-reworked headline route trace is a separate project.

Any future attempt must retain paired per-token routes, or freeze a replacement
contract before seeing new data, and pass the unchanged action-output, CE,
identity, state, gradient, and finiteness rules with zero unexplained route
changes. Route explanation alone cannot retroactively validate this pair or its
`14.22793536158026` timing observation.

MarinSkyRL #276 remains unchanged and green at `0c213586`; local candidate
`fbb1fc8` was not pushed. I am leaving #7903 open for any future R3/live-route
work, but the bounded question for this cycle is settled: FP32 combine
accumulation is a real fixed-route correction and is not sufficient for
production acceptance.

The exact local candidate patch, frozen launchers/runners/readers, monitor, and
reader summaries are preserved in the
[evidence-only commit](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/7c3bac451a69d34fa8b8f027ceb91998a6e0ff2c).

It does **not** exonerate grouped MoE for every run or trajectory, and it does not identify attention as the cause. The original failed gate still controls.

Per the frozen stop rule, I did not retry, weaken the tolerance, attempt an unsupported correction, or launch a final clean pair. Targeted CPU validation passed 26 tests, plus `py_compile`, Ruff, shellcheck, launcher/readback dry-runs, and `git diff --check`. The 32-H100 probe used at most 115.63 GiB cgroup memory on any task, host available memory stayed above 1.848 TiB, and swap stayed at zero. Its head task completed and produced the durable artifact; three followers that remained in teardown were explicitly stopped after independent readback, releasing the allocation.

Recommendation for #276: keep `fbb1fc8` off the PR. It failed the unchanged semantic contract and this follow-up found no localized cause that supports a correction. Leave #276 at its current head for human review; adopting `fbb1fc8` would require a separate, explicit contract justification and new evidence, not reinterpretation of this failed run.

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Build a Zephyr pipeline that turns DOCX records in Common Crawl WARCs into Marin [`NormalizedData`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/normalize.py). Use the PDF extraction step in #7618 as a model.

Use [DocxCorpus](https://github.com/superdoc/docx-corpus) as a reference for two operations. It uses Docling to map DOCX files to text. It uses lingua for language identification (LID). Its classifiers, embeddings, storage service, API, and user interface are out of scope.

DocxCorpus reports [1,101,537 uploaded files and 736,242 classified files](https://docxcorp.us/dataset). It has extracted only a fraction of the DOCX files in Common Crawl. The Marin pipeline must read Common Crawl indexes. It must not use the DocxCorpus manifest as its source list.

Reuse the WARC range fetch and provenance fields from [`focus_crawl.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/focus_crawl.py).

### Definition of Done

- A Zephyr step reads DOCX candidates from a selected Common Crawl index. The query uses MIME and URL data.
- The step fetches each WARC record, validates the DOCX container, extracts text, and detects the language.
- The output keeps the crawl ID, source URL, WARC path, offset, length, text, and language.
- The step writes valid `NormalizedData`.
- Counters report valid files, invalid files, empty text, and extraction errors.
- Tests cover valid, malformed, empty, and multilingual DOCX fixtures.
- A sample run reports extraction yield and includes a manual text review.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md, fix-issue and commit skills
- [x] Actionability check — actionable (clear Definition of Done)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PR/issue overlaps)
- [x] Research codebase (index/WARC/normalize path)
- [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach
- [ ] Human review of approach before implementation (feature is >100 LOC, multi-module, new deps → no PR yet)

# Research

Scope is a **new** production pipeline, not a bug fix: read a Common Crawl columnar index for DOCX candidates, range-fetch each WARC record, validate the OOXML container, extract text (Docling), detect language (lingua), and write `NormalizedData`. Two existing pieces matter. `docx_corpus.py` already ingests DocxCorpus but pulls pre-extracted text from that site's manifest — exactly the source this issue forbids; it is not the model. The model is the archived `focus_crawl.py`, whose WARC range-fetch + provenance code was **removed from HEAD** (`common_crawl_focus.py` now only reads the finished artifact), so its helpers must be resurrected into a shared module before reuse.

**Relevant code**
- [`normalize.py#L70`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/normalize.py#L70) — `NormalizedData` target schema
- [`docx_corpus.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/docx_corpus.py) — manifest-based DocxCorpus ingest (forbidden source; not the template)
- [`common_crawl_focus.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/common_crawl_focus.py) — reads finished focus-crawl artifact
- [`focus_crawl.py@20b7003fe`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20b7003fea217ec031c0cfe77643854641abbffc/experiments/datakit/focus_crawl.py) — archived WARC range-fetch + provenance (gone from HEAD): `focus_crawl_warc_paths`, `_download_range`, `iter_warc_text_records`, `_OUTPUT_SCHEMA`
- [`pyproject.toml#L197`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/pyproject.toml#L197) — `datakit` dep group (no docling/lingua/warcio yet)

# Proposed Approach

Feature-sized (new module, new deps, fixtures, sample run) — well over the 100-line PR threshold, so this is for review before code lands. Mirror the focus-crawl → `common_crawl_focus` split: production module under `lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/`, not an `experiments/` script.

1. **Shared WARC base.** Lift the archived range-fetch helpers into `common_crawl_warc.py` (session/retry, `_cdx_path`, `_download_range`, container-record iteration). Generalize `iter_warc_text_records` to take a MIME predicate + extractor callable so this DOCX step and the PDF step (#7618) share one base instead of copy-pasting the deleted experiment file.
2. **Index query (MIME + URL).** New `common_crawl_docx.py` reads a selected crawl's columnar cc-index (`cc-index/table/cc-main/warc`), filtering on `content_mime_type`/`content_mime_detected` == `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document` and/or a `.docx` URL suffix, yielding `(warc_filename, offset, length, url)`. `duckdb` (already a datakit dep) over the parquet index is the natural fit; the index supplies exact per-record offset/length, so fetch that single gzip member rather than focus-crawl's coalesced HTML ranges. Explicitly **not** the DocxCorpus manifest.
3. **Validate container.** OOXML DOCX is a zip; open bytes with `zipfile` and require `word/document.xml`. Reject others → `invalid_files` counter.
4. **Extract text.** Docling `DocumentConverter` on the validated bytes. Guard extraction failures → `extraction_errors`; blank output → `empty_text`.
5. **Language ID.** lingua on extracted text → `language`.
6. **Output.** Schema: `id, text, source_id` (WARC-Record-ID), `source` (crawl id), `url, warc_filename, warc_offset, warc_length, language`, `version`. Write via the focus-crawl `write_parquet` + `NormalizedData` pattern.
7. **Counters.** `valid_files, invalid_files, empty_text, extraction_errors` (+ per-language tally).
8. **Deps.** Add `docling`, `lingua-language-detector`, and `warcio` (previously a lazy import) to the `datakit` group.
9. **Tests** (`tests/datakit/download/test_common_crawl_docx.py`, no mocks): build in-fixture DOCX bytes (valid, malformed-zip, empty-body, non-English) and assert validate/extract/LID outcomes and counter deltas from local bytes — no network.
10. **Sample run.** Small stratified slice of one crawl index; report extraction yield + a manual text-review snippet back on this issue.

**Open questions for the reviewer**
- Which crawl/index snapshot to target first (a `CC-MAIN-YYYY-WW` columnar index vs. a supplemental)?
- OK to add `docling` + `lingua` to the `datakit` extra given their footprint, or keep them lazy-imported like `warcio`/`justext`?
- Should the shared `common_crawl_warc.py` refactor land as its own PR ahead of the DOCX step (it also unblocks #7618)?

spillover_issues.author: wmoss
spillover_issues.body:
#### **Context & Goal**
Currently, Zephyr data pipeline steps are defined in Python using operators like `map_step`, `flat_map_step`, and `reduce_step`. To support high-performance distributed SQL execution via DataFusion/Ballista, we want to introduce a first-class `.sql` operator in Zephyr that accepts SQL query strings or `.sql` files and executes them over dataset partitions.

---

#### **Key Considerations to Address**

* **File I/O Integration**: How does the `.sql` operator interact with loading and writing files? Is file loading and output serialization handled natively within SQL (e.g., `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE ... LOCATION ...` and `COPY TO ...`), or handled by Zephyr's reader/writer stages?
* **Stage Boundary Isolation**: Does Zephyr always consider a `.sql` operator as a separate, distinct stage with reading and writing from GCS as its interface?
* **Execution Engine Dispatch**: How does the `.sql` operator dispatch queries between local DataFusion (for single-node execution) and the distributed Ballista cluster on Iris?
* **Metadata & Schema Propagation**: How are dataset schema validation, row counts, and output metadata passed through the `.sql` stage to downstream Zephyr operators?

---

#### **Proposed Tasks**

* [ ] **Operator API**: Define the user-facing syntax for registering `.sql` steps in Zephyr pipelines (e.g., `sql_step(...)`).
* [ ] **Execution Handler**: Implement the stage executor that bridges Zephyr task specs to DataFusion / Ballista execution contexts.
* [ ] **Integration Tests**: Add end-to-end test coverage running `.sql` stages in Zephyr pipelines over Parquet/NdJson datasets on GCS.

spillover_issues.author: ayush1298
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 Related to the evals wish-list in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7090 (item 12). Proposing a procedurally generated, difficulty-parameterized proxy for SciCode. This issue is a design proposal only. I'd like agreement on scope and on the questions at the bottom before writing the generator.

Of the four proxy items (10–13), SciCode is the only one that is (a) graded programmatically with no judge model, (b) amenable to procedural instance generation with provably correct gold answers, and (c) validatable end-to-end on modest compute.

Briefly, why not the others yet:

- **GDPval-AA v2 (10)** — needs expert/LLM grading of open-ended deliverables plus an agentic shell+browse scaffold.
- **𝜏³-Banking (11)** — needs a user-simulator LLM per episode; sub-8B models floor on multi-turn tool use, so there is no rank signal at the scales we can cheaply validate against.
- **AA-Omniscience (13)** — its index rewards abstention, but small instruct models essentially never abstain, so the index degenerates to `2·accuracy − 1` and the calibration axis (the point of the benchmark) disappears during validation.

## The problem with SciCode as-is

SciCode is 338 subproblems from 80 main problems. At publication, the best model solved ~4.6% of main problems in the most realistic setting. A benchmark where the frontier scores single-digit and near-zero pass rates also mean near-zero information per item, so distinguishing two checkpoints needs an impractical number of samples.

The proxy's job is therefore not "SciCode but easier." It is:

> One generator and one difficulty dial such that a ~300M model sits in the sensitive band at low difficulty, a frontier model sits in the sensitive band at high difficulty, and **model ordering is preserved along the whole dial**.

## Design

### Three response modes

Same underlying item, three regimes — so one dataset serves in-loop pretraining evals *and* post-hoc generation evals:

| Mode | Format | Scoring path | Signal range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M** | multiple-choice over candidate implementations | logprob → runs **in-loop** via the Levanter harness | ~150M–1B |
| **F** | full function given, one line masked | short generation | ~1B–7B |
| **G** | write the function from the description (SciCode-native) | generation + unit tests | 7B–frontier |

### Difficulty as a vector, not a scalar

Independent axes so we can ablate which one actually drives ranking; scalar presets `D1…D5` are fixed combinations.

| Axis | Range |
|---|---|
| `d_chain` | 1 → 6 dependent subproblems |
| `d_scaffold` | L3 formula + shapes + worked example · L2 background prose · L1 terse signature (SciCode "no background") · L0 main problem only, model decomposes |
| `d_derive` | formula given / one step away / must be derived |
| `d_numeric` | benign inputs, `rtol=1e-3` → stiff, ill-conditioned, boundary-edge, `rtol=1e-8` |
| `d_libs` | scipy allowed → numpy only → pure Python |
| `d_noise` | irrelevant prior functions injected into context |

### Metrics

- SciCode-native: **subproblem pass rate** (gold prior steps injected) and **main-problem pass rate** (all-or-nothing, model's own prior steps).
- Proxy-native: **`D50`** — difficulty level at which pass rate crosses 50%, from a logistic fit to the pass-rate-vs-difficulty curve. Scale-free and immune to both floor and ceiling effects.
- Reported separately: **format-failure rate** (unparseable output), so we can tell a genuine capability signal from markdown compliance.

### v0 task families

Mirroring 4 SciCode's categories (numerical methods/simulation / scientific calculation):

- `numcalc` — quadrature, root finding, finite-difference derivatives, Richardson extrapolation
- `ode` — Euler / RK4 / velocity-Verlet / symplectic Euler on harmonic oscillator, damped-driven pendulum, Lotka–Volterra, SIR, Kepler two-body
- `numla` — Gram–Schmidt, power iteration, Jacobi/Gauss–Seidel, Thomas tridiagonal solver, Householder QR
- `quantum1d` — finite-difference Schrödinger: build D², build H, ground state, expectation values; box / harmonic / double-well / Pöschl–Teller potentials

Some other things as well, that we can use if we were not able to get good quality samples in v0: PDE finite-difference, thin-film transfer matrices, tight-binding band structure, Ising Metropolis, Needleman–Wunsch, DFT/PSD.

### Generation

Per family, not per instance: `sample_spec(rng, difficulty)` → `reference(spec)` → `render_prompt(spec, difficulty)` → `make_tests(spec, rng)`. Test outputs are produced by running the reference, so tests are correct by construction and instances are unlimited.

**Two-implementation gate.** No instance ships unless the reference agrees with an independent source to ≥2 orders of magnitude tighter than the test tolerance — RK4 vs `solve_ivp`, harmonic-well FD Schrödinger vs analytic `E0 = ½ħω`, Gram–Schmidt vs `np.linalg.qr`, Simpson vs `scipy.integrate.quad`. This replaces scientist annotation as the correctness guarantee.

**Determinism.** Explicit seeds; pinned shape/dtype/ordering/sign/units asserted before value comparison; no wall-clock, network, or ordering-dependent structures; 5s per-test timeout; `np.allclose` with both `rtol` and `atol`; CI runs every gold solution through the grader and requires 100% pass.

**Contamination.** Randomized identifiers and parameters mean no verbatim string exists upstream. Dataset carries a canary GUID. Memorization probe: check whether a strong model reproduces the reference verbatim on a canonicalized (non-randomized) variant; if so, that family needs more randomization.


### Difficulty analysis

Difficulty analysis across four layers, cheapest first.

#### (a) Empirical difficulty curves

Pass rate vs. each axis, per model. Fit a 2-parameter logistic and report **`D50`** (difficulty at 50% pass rate) and the **slope**. Slope matters as much as location — a flat curve means the knob does nothing and the axis should be dropped or redesigned.

#### (b) Item Response Theory (2PL)

Fit `P(correct | model m, item i) = σ(a_i (θ_m − b_i))` by marginal maximum likelihood over the full model × item matrix. Three outputs, each doing real work:

- **`b_i` — item difficulty** on a common latent scale, so items from different families become directly comparable. This is what lets us claim the scalar presets D1–D5 mean the same thing across `numcalc` and `quantum1d`.
- **`a_i` — item discrimination.** The screening tool. Low-`a` items fail to separate models regardless of how hard they are, and get cut from the frozen set. This is how we avoid shipping 600 items where 200 carry the signal.
- **`θ_m` — model ability**, the natural quantity to correlate against SciCode instead of a raw pass rate.

Fitting is seconds on CPU (`py-irt`, or EM in numpy) — the constraint is having **per-item** results, not compute.

#### (c) Axis attribution

Mixed-effects logistic regression on item-level outcomes:

```
correct ~ d_chain + d_scaffold + d_derive + d_numeric + d_libs + d_noise
          + (1 | model) + (1 | family) + (1 | problem)
```

Coefficients quantify how much each knob actually moves difficulty; random effects prevent one badly-calibrated family from driving the fit. Report standardized effect sizes so axes are comparable. This is also the check against the "proxy measures numpy fluency, not science" risk — we want `d_derive` and `d_scaffold` carrying weight, not `d_libs` alone.

#### (d) Validation of the dial

Three preregistered checks:

- **Monotonicity** — pass rate non-increasing in each axis, per model.
- **Ordering stability** — model ordering preserved across ≥3 consecutive difficulty levels (Kendall τ between adjacent levels).
- **No axis inverts** — no axis where increasing difficulty *helps* some model class, which would indicate the knob measures format compliance rather than capability.

#### (e) Decomposing knowledge vs. implementation

Two mechanisms, neither requiring a judge model, both falling out of owning the reference implementation.

**Dual grading.** Score each response twice: strictly (`np.allclose`), and again under a *declared* convention group — sign/phase, scalar unit factor, eigenvalue ordering, transpose, 0-vs-1 indexing. The gap between the two scores is the **implementation tax**. A model at 30% strict and 55% tolerant knew the science and lost 25 points to conventions.

**Automatic error taxonomy.** Failures classify themselves:

| Code | Failure | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| E0 | no parseable code | format |
| E1 | syntax / import error | format |
| E2 | runtime exception | implementation |
| E3 | wrong shape or dtype | implementation |
| E4 | right shape, values far off | **knowledge** — wrong algorithm |
| E5 | right shape, close but outside tolerance | **implementation** — convention, units, off-by-one, precision |

The **E4:E5 ratio** gives a knowledge-vs-implementation split per model and per difficulty level, at no extra cost.

**Factorial isolation.** The axes are manipulable independently, so:

- *Knowledge held out, implementation varied:* fix `d_derive = 0` (formula given verbatim), sweep `d_numeric` and convention strictness.
- *Implementation held trivial, knowledge varied:* one-line function body, no shape juggling, sweep `d_scaffold` L3 → L0 and `d_derive` 0 → 2.

Collapse in the first sweep implies implementation dominates; collapse in the second implies knowledge does. An interaction is the likely and most interesting outcome.

#### Reporting discipline

Format-failure rate (E0 + E1) is reported separately throughout, never folded into the headline. If it exceeds ~10% for a model, that model's scores are not interpretable and it is **excluded** from the correlation rather than quietly averaged in.

---

## Validation plan

We want to ensure that model rank correlation should hold w.r.t. original SciCode at substantially lower cost. Protocol:

1. **Preregister** model roster, difficulty presets, prompt template, and target metric in this issue before any correlation is computed.
2. **Dev / held-out split by family.** Tune presets on `numcalc` + `ode`; report final correlation on `numla` + `quantum1d` only.
3. **Measure the reference directly.** Run original SciCode on the roster (288 test-set subproblems, short outputs, CPU-only grading — tractable at these model sizes) rather than relying solely on published leaderboard numbers. Use published numbers as a secondary external anchor.
4. **Roster, two groups.**
   - *Scaling ladders (validity check — true order known a priori):* Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5B→1.5B→3B→7B; Llama-3.2-1B→3.2-3B→3.1-8B
   - *Cross-family spread:* Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, Gemma-2-2B, Phi-3.5-mini, SmolLM2-1.7B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-4B/8B, **Marin-8B-Instruct**
5. **Statistics.** Spearman ρ and Kendall τ_b, with bootstrap CIs resampled over models *and* over items. Plus **pairwise order agreement restricted to model pairs whose reference scores differ by more than their combined 95% CI** — correlating against noise otherwise inflates ρ.
6. **Acceptance targets:** held-out ρ ≥ 0.90; pairwise agreement ≥ 0.85; monotone recovery of both scaling ladders across ≥3 consecutive difficulty levels.
7. **Cost claim, quantified.** Report `n_80%` — items needed for 80% power to detect the observed gap at α=0.05 — for SciCode vs. the proxy at matched difficulty, alongside token counts, wall-clock, and per-item curation cost.

## Scope

**In scope for v0:** 4 families × 5 difficulty levels × ~30 instances (~600 items) plus Mode M variants; harness-agnostic generator + scorer; frozen JSONL snapshot; validation report.

**Out of scope for v0:** additional families, paper-derived "realism tier," multi-language support, RL/training use.

## Milestones

- [ ] Design agreed (this issue)
- [ ] Generator interface + `numcalc` end-to-end + sandboxed grader + CI gold-solution check
- [ ] Remaining three families, two-implementation gate applied, v0 snapshot frozen
- [ ] Reference SciCode measured across roster
- [ ] Proxy sweep, presets tuned on dev families only
- [ ] Held-out correlation + D50 curves + power analysis + memorization probes
- [ ] PR: generator, dataset, scorer, harness wiring, docs, validation report

## Some questions:

1. **What model scale must show signal?** Does this need to discriminate ~300M ablation checkpoints, or is 8B+ sufficient? This determines whether Mode M is essential or optional.
2. **Which harness should it land in** — evalchemy post-hoc, Harbor, or a custom evaluator under `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators`? I plan to keep the generator and scorer harness-agnostic either way.
3. **Is a code-execution sandbox available in the eval path** as Numerical tolerances depend on versions of different libraries like numpy/scipy.
4. Is cluster time available if I want to run > 8B models?

The multidimensional vector evaluation looks great. 

There are results from more recent models in 
[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/scicode) and [LLM Registry](https://llm-registry.com/benchmark/scicode?view=all&variants=0&range=all), are they in the same scale compared to the original set?

comments.author: ayush1298
comments.body:
@Nativeatom, below are answers to your questions as per my analysis: 

## 1. Same scale as the paper?

No. The paper's **4.6%** is **main-problem** accuracy — all-or-nothing over a chain, using the model's own prior steps. AA's ~60% is the **subproblem** metric over the 288 test-set subproblems. Different denominator and aggregation.

**LLM Registry isn't a second data point** as it lists AA as its source and the numbers match (Gemini 3.1 Pro 59.0% vs 58.9%). 

**The bigger issue is compression.** Median 44%, top three within 1.5 points. At n=288 the SE at p=0.6 is 2.9pp — and subproblems are nested in 80 main problems, so at ICC 0.2 effective n is ~190 and SE rises to ~3.6pp. Minimum detectable difference on unpaired aggregates is **~11pp**. The top of that leaderboard is one statistical tie.

Two consequences: run the reference ourselves for **per-item** results, since paired comparison is far more powerful than the above; and restrict the correlation target to model pairs actually separated in the reference, or ρ is attenuated and uninterpretable.

It also sharpens the motivation that SciCode has a **floor problem at small scale** *and* a **ceiling-compression problem at the frontier**, which is why the headline metric is `D50` rather than a raw pass rate.

## 2. Scientific Knowledge or snippet implementation?

**Both, binding at different scales.** Knowledge gates whether a small model attempts the right algorithm at all; implementation thoroughness is what's compressing the top.

The Ewald example on AA's own page: all four energy terms are given in full LaTeX, so barely any derivation remains. What's left is broadcasting bookkeeping (`(natoms, npairs, 1, 3)` against `(natoms, 1, ncells, 3)`), an exclusion rule stated purely as boundary conditions, and unit discipline (zJ / nm/ps / g·mol⁻¹, `kB = 0.0138064852 zJ/K`, a g/mol → kg/particle conversion). A model can know exactly what Ewald summation is and fail all of it.

On the contrary, EAIRA's SciCode analysis found significant gains from supplying scientific background, which reads as a real reasoning limit rather than a coding one.

So rather than assert a winner, the proposal now includes two mechanisms that measure the split directly, neither needing a judge model . **dual grading** (strict vs. convention-tolerant; the gap is the implementation tax) and an **automatic error taxonomy** separating "right shape, values far off" (knowledge — wrong algorithm) from "right shape, outside tolerance" (implementation — convention, units, off-by-one). That ratio gives the split per model and per difficulty level. My prediction is that it flips from knowledge- to implementation-dominated somewhere in the 3–7B range.

comments.author: rfgordan
comments.body:
There are a lot of cool ideas here. 

A couple thoughts on the goals of this work, related to your last question: 

> What model scale must show signal? Does this need to discriminate ~300M ablation checkpoints, or is 8B+ sufficient? This determines whether Mode M is essential or optional.

My understanding is that the critical piece here is discriminating the post-training checkpoints (I believe I've seen RL experiments down to 1B). I think the pretraining metrics can be deferred to future work. Also, in the validation plan here its called out that the eval should be "substantially lower cost". I think cost is a nice property but it's not highlighted as a primary goal in the Epic.

With that in mind, I would consider what the minimum viable version of this that still discriminates at lower scales would be. For example, Mode G + the first three difficulty vectors are quite intuitive as easier versions of SciCode, so require a little bit less faith in the statistical machinery proposed here. Worth testing how low you can go with just those. Relatedly, with something like the D50 metric, I'd be worried that there may be some reliance on properties of the underlying scaling curve that aren't guaranteed.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
The marin SFT launcher (`experiments/sft/`) has two latent bugs on the **GPU (CoreWeave H100)** path that block a full-parameter SFT of any non-trivial checkpoint. Both surfaced running a 25B dense SFT (`delphi-1e23`) on a single `8xH100` node, and both are specific to the GPU path — the recipe was previously validated only on TPU, where `ResourceConfig.with_tpu` sizes the host from the slice, so neither was ever exercised. The training child dies before completing a step in both cases. Suggested fixes below (the first is already applied in a working tree and can be upstreamed as-is).

## Bug 1 — GPU pod gets no host RAM, OOMs during `initialize_from_hf`

`experiments/sft/launcher.py::resources_from_accelerator` built the GPU `ResourceConfig` with `with_gpu(variant, count=..., regions=[ANY_REGION])` and **no `ram=`/`cpu=`/`disk=`**, so it inherited the `ResourceConfig` default of ~4 GB host RAM. `initialize_from_hf` buffers the entire HF state dict in **host RAM** before device placement (Levanter `_load_from_remote`); a 25B fp32 checkpoint is ~100 GB, so the child is `SIGKILL`ed reading the first ~2.8 GB shard. The failure is silent — no traceback, just an OOMKill — and Iris surfaces the last-flushed stdout line as a misleading "reason", so it reads like a checkpoint/IO error rather than host-RAM exhaustion.

**Suggested fix (applied, working):** size host cpu/ram/disk with the GPU count in the GPU branch, mirroring what `with_tpu` already does per slice. The node (`gd-8xh100ib-i128`) is 128 vCPU / 2 TB, so per-device 8 vCPU / 96 GB / 48 GB (→ `8xH100` = 64 vCPU / 768 GB / 384 GB) is comfortable headroom:

```python
_GPU_HOST_CPU_PER_DEVICE = 8
_GPU_HOST_RAM_GB_PER_DEVICE = 96
_GPU_HOST_DISK_GB_PER_DEVICE = 48

def resources_from_accelerator(accelerator: str) -> ResourceConfig:
    gpu = _GPU_ACCELERATOR.fullmatch(accelerator)
    if gpu is not None:
        count = int(gpu["count"])
        return ResourceConfig.with_gpu(
            gpu["variant"], count=count, regions=[ANY_REGION],
            cpu=_GPU_HOST_CPU_PER_DEVICE * count,
            ram=f"{_GPU_HOST_RAM_GB_PER_DEVICE * count}g",
            disk=f"{_GPU_HOST_DISK_GB_PER_DEVICE * count}g",
        )
    return ResourceConfig.with_tpu(accelerator)
```

(Resources are a runtime arg excluded from the step fingerprint, so this does not fork any cached artifact.)

## Bug 2 — tokenizer staging rejects `s3://`/`gs://` paths (`HFValidationError`)

When a `ModelSource` resolves the tokenizer path to an object-store dir (e.g. `PreparedModel`, whose `tokenizer_path = ctx.artifact_path(step)` is `s3://…` / `gs://…`), the SFT dies **before compile** with:

```
HFValidationError: Repo id must be in the form '.../...' … 's3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/checkpoints/delphi-1e23-prepared/2026.07.19'
```

The **weights** path handles URL-like ids: `compat/hf_checkpoints.py` routes `if "://" in id` through fsspec (`_load_state_dict` ~L752) and loads the HF config under `_patch_hf_hub_download()` (~L1599), whose `custom_validate_repo_id` bypasses `validate_repo_id` for `_is_url_like` ids (~L1306). But the **tokenizer** staging path does not: `levanter/tokenizers.py::load_tokenizer` (~L732) → `_stage_tokenizer` → `_stage_from_hf` (~L857) calls `huggingface_hub.snapshot_download(name_or_path, allow_patterns=…)` (~L868) **with no `_is_url_like` guard and outside `_patch_hf_hub_download()`**, so `validate_repo_id` rejects the object-store dir.

**Suggested fix:** in `levanter/tokenizers.py`, add a `_is_url_like` check so URL-like tokenizer paths are fetched via fsspec (download the tokenizer files from the `s3://`/`gs://` dir) instead of being handed raw to `snapshot_download`/`validate_repo_id` — or, minimally, wrap the `snapshot_download` in the same `_patch_hf_hub_download()` context the weights path uses so the URL bypass applies uniformly. Either makes the tokenizer path consistent with the already-URL-aware weights path.

**Current workaround** (does not need the fix): point the SFT `ModelSource` at an HF **repo id** rather than an object-store dir (the `HFModel(model_ref=<hf repo>)` path, which the proven `delphi_1e22` config uses). That is why `PreparedModel(step=…)` — designed to init from a prep-step's object-store output — is unusable on this path today.

## Impact / scope

- Bug 1 affects **every** GPU SFT of a checkpoint whose host-RAM state dict exceeds ~4 GB (i.e. anything past a small model), independent of dataset.
- Bug 2 affects any `ModelSource` that resolves the tokenizer to an `s3://`/`gs://` dir — notably `PreparedModel`, making the reproducible "prep-step → init-from-step-output" flow unusable on GPU/CoreWeave until fixed; the HF-repo staging workaround is the only path today.

Both are in the `experiments/sft/` + Levanter tokenizer-staging code and were confirmed by an end-to-end 25B `8xH100` run that, once both were addressed, compiles and trains cleanly (first step 30.9 s, ~4.3 s/it).
